title: Bisaya grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Bisaya, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Bisaya as people say it in Cebu, written the way the Basics course writes it.

units.title: Doing things to things and people

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them back: your first Bisaya conversation.
lessons.topic: Sentences without “am, is, are”; {{ako}} / {{ko}} “I”, {{ikaw}} / {{ka}} “you”; {{si}} before a name; {{taga-}} “from”

goal.t: Maayong buntag! Ako si Ana. Taga-Cebu ko.
goal.tr: Good morning! I'm Ana. I'm from Cebu.

dialog.tr: Good morning! I'm Ben.

dialog.t: Maayong buntag, Ben. Ako si Ana.
dialog.tr: Good morning, Ben. I'm Ana.
Where are you from, Ana?
I'm from Cebu. And you?
I'm from America. I'm a student here.
Nice to meet you!

blocks.p: Look at what is missing: Bisaya has no word for “am”, “is” or “are”. {{Taga-Cebu ko}} is, word for word, “from-Cebu I”, and {{Estudyante ko}} is “student I”. And the order is the other way round from English: **what you are comes first, then who**.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Cebu.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **Two words for “I”, two for “you”.** {{ako}} and {{ikaw}} are the full words: they start a sentence or stand alone ({{Ako si Ana.}} {{Ikaw?}}). {{ko}} and {{ka}} are short and can never start a sentence: they go **right after the first word** ({{Taga-Cebu ko.}} {{Taga-asa ka?}}).

**{{si}} before a name.** A person's name has the little word {{si}} in front of it: {{Ako si Ana.}} “I'm Ana.” It has no English translation; it just says “a name comes next”. And {{taga-}} before a place means “from”: {{taga-Cebu}}, {{taga-Amerika}}, and {{Taga-asa ka?}} “Where are you from?”

ex.note: said by a woman; a man says {{maestro}}
a question just by raising your voice at the end

blocks.tip: {{Maayong buntag}} “good morning”, {{maayong udto}} “good noon”, {{maayong hapon}} “good afternoon”, {{maayong gabii}} “good evening”. Bisaya has no special polite word: you show respect with Sir and Ma'am, or {{Nang}} (to an older woman) and {{Nong}} (to an older man).

mistakes.why: {{ko}} is a short word: it can't start a sentence, it goes after the first word.
Put {{si}} before a person's name.

practice.why: What you are comes first, then the short {{ko}}. ({{Taga-Cebu ka}} is “you're from Cebu”.)

practice.q: You're Tom, from Canada. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{ako}}. ({{Ikaw si Tom}} is “you're Tom”.)

practice.q: Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Maayong…}}

answers.tr: Good morning! I'm John. I'm from America.

lessons.title: Say what people and things are like
lessons.summary: Say that the coffee is hot, Cebu is beautiful and your friend is kind, with every “he”, “she”, “we” and “they”.
lessons.topic: The describing word first; {{ang}} and {{si}} for who or what you mean; {{siya}}, {{kami}}, {{kita}}, {{kamo}}, {{sila}}; {{kaayo}} “very”

goal.t: Nindot kaayo ang Cebu!
goal.tr: Cebu is really beautiful!

dialog.tr: How's Cebu, Ben?

dialog.t: Nindot kaayo ang Cebu! Pero init.
dialog.tr: Cebu is really beautiful! But hot.
Yes, it's really hot today.
Who's she?

dialog.t: Si Maria. Maestra siya. Buotan kaayo siya.
dialog.tr: That's Maria. She's a teacher. She's really kind.
She's pretty too.

blocks.p: The same pattern as the last lesson: **the describing word first, then who or what**, and no “is”. {{Buotan siya}} is “kind she”; {{Init ang kape}} is “hot the coffee”.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: hot, kind, beautiful, big.

blocks.p: **{{ang}} and {{si}}.** When you name the thing or person you're talking about, put a little word before it: {{ang}} before a thing, a place or a person in general ({{ang kape}} “the coffee”, {{ang Cebu}}), {{si}} before a person's name ({{si Maria}}). They point at **who or what the sentence is about**. {{ang}} is often “the” in English, but it goes before place names too: {{Nindot ang Cebu.}} “Cebu is beautiful.”

blocks.means: a little word in front of a noun that shows its job in the sentence. {{ang}} and {{si}} mark who or what the sentence is about; more markers come later.

blocks.p: **Every person.** Here are all the words for “I, you, he, she, we, they”. Two things are new for an English speaker: {{siya}} is **he and she** (Bisaya doesn't say which), and there are **two words for “we”**: {{kami}} leaves out the person you're talking to, {{kita}} includes them.
**{{kaayo}} “very”** comes after the describing word: {{init kaayo}} “very hot”, {{nindot kaayo}} “really beautiful”.

ex.tr: He's a doctor. / She's a doctor.
ex.note: {{siya}} is he or she: the situation tells you which
no word for “it”: everyone knows what you mean

blocks.tip: “It” usually isn't said at all: {{Init!}} “It's hot!”, {{Lami!}} “It's tasty!”.

mistakes.why: Bisaya puts the describing word first, then the thing it describes.
A name needs {{si}} in front of it.

practice.why: Bisaya has one word for both: {{siya}}.
A thing has {{ang}} before it; {{si}} is for names.

practice.q: Your turn: say what your city, a friend or your food is like. Use {{kaayo}}.

answers.tr: Chicago is really beautiful, but cold.

answers.t: Buotan kaayo si Mark.
answers.tr: Mark is really kind.

answers.t: Lami kaayo ang pagkaon dinhi.
answers.tr: The food here is really delicious.

lessons.title: Ask simple questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions with {{ba}}, and ask who, what and where.
lessons.topic: {{ba}} for yes-or-no questions; {{unsa}}, {{kinsa}}, {{asa}}, {{taga-asa}}; {{man}}; {{unsay}}, {{kinsay}}

goal.t: Taga-asa ka? Estudyante ka ba?
goal.tr: Where are you from? Are you a student?

dialog.tr: Good evening! What's your name?
Emma. And you?

dialog.t: Ako si Lito. Taga-asa ka, Emma?
dialog.tr: I'm Lito. Where are you from, Emma?
I'm from Australia.
Are you a tourist?
Yes. So where's the Basilica?
It's really close!

blocks.p: **Yes or no.** Take an ordinary sentence and add {{ba}} after the first word and its short word: {{Turista ka.}} “You're a tourist.” → {{Turista ka ba?}} “Are you a tourist?” You can also just raise your voice at the end, without {{ba}}. The answer is {{Oo}} “yes”.
**Who, what, where.** The question word comes **first**, and the short word ({{ka}}, {{ko}}) right after it: {{Taga-asa ka?}} “Where are you from?”

**Two handy shortcuts.** {{unsa ang}} is often said {{unsay}}, and {{kinsa ang}} {{kinsay}}: {{Unsay imong ngalan?}} And {{man}} after the question word makes a question softer and friendlier, a little like “so…?”: {{Asa man ang banyo?}} “So where's the bathroom?”

blocks.tip: Where does {{ba}} go? After the short words {{ko}}, {{ka}}, {{mi}}, {{ta}}, {{mo}} ({{Turista ka ba?}}), but before the longer {{siya}}, {{sila}} and names ({{Turista ba siya?}} {{Naa ba si Ben?}}).

mistakes.why: {{ka}} and {{ba}} never come first: they follow the first word.
The question word comes first, then {{ka}}.

practice.q: Which little word turns {{Taga-Cebu ka}} into a yes-or-no question?

lines.why: Answer, then ask back with {{Ikaw?}} ({{Kinsa ka?}} “who are you?” sounds rude here.)

answers.tr: What's your name? Where are you from?

lessons.title: Say no and set things straight
lessons.summary: Say what you're not (“I'm not American, I'm from Canada”) and answer no politely.
lessons.topic: {{dili}} “not, no”; the short word moves to right after {{dili}}; {{oo}} and {{dili}}

goal.t: Dili ko Amerikano. Taga-Canada ko.
goal.tr: I'm not American. I'm from Canada.

dialog.tr: Are you American, Sir?

dialog.t: Dili, dili ko Amerikano. Taga-Canada ko.
dialog.tr: No, I'm not American. I'm from Canada.
Oh, sorry! Are you a tourist?

dialog.t: Dili. Maestro ko dinhi sa Cebu.
dialog.tr: No. I'm a teacher here in Cebu.
You're a teacher? Nice!

blocks.p: {{dili}} is “not”, and on its own, “no”. Put it **in front of** the describing word: {{Amerikano ko}} “I'm American” → {{Dili ko Amerikano}} “I'm not American”.

**Watch the short word move.** {{ko}} always goes right after the first word of the sentence. When {{dili}} comes in, {{dili}} is the first word, so {{ko}} jumps to just after it: {{Dili ko Amerikano}}, not {{Dili Amerikano ko}}. The same with {{ka}}, {{mi}}, {{ta}}, and the longer {{siya}} and {{sila}} too.

table: {{Dili siya maestra.}} She's not a teacher.
{{Init ang kape.}} The coffee is hot.
{{Dili init ang kape.}} The coffee isn't hot.

blocks.tip: Bisaya has a second word for “no”, {{wala}}, for “there isn't any” and for things that didn't happen. It comes in the next unit. For who and what someone or something is, it's always {{dili}}.

mistakes.why: {{ko}} goes right after the first word, and now the first word is {{dili}}.
A sentence can't start with {{ko}}: start with {{dili}}.

practice.q: Someone in Cebu guesses wrong about you. Set them straight.

lines.why: You're not from Manila, so start with {{Dili}}.

practice.q: Someone asks you {{Estudyante ka ba?}} You're a teacher. You answer…
Your turn: say one thing you're not and one thing you are.

answers.t: Dili ko Amerikano. Taga-England ko.
answers.tr: I'm not American. I'm from England.

answers.t: Dili ko maestra. Doktor ko.
answers.tr: I'm not a teacher. I'm a doctor.

answers.t: Dili ko gigutom, pero gikapoy ko.
answers.tr: I'm not hungry, but I'm tired.

lessons.title: Point at things and ask what they are
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this? What's that?” at the market, and introduce someone with “This is…”.
lessons.topic: {{kini}}, {{kana}}, {{kadto}} (short {{ni}}, {{na}}, {{to}}); {{Mao ni…}}; {{Unsa ni?}}

goal.t: Unsa kana? Lami ba?
goal.tr: What's that? Is it tasty?

dialog.tr: What's that?
These are lanzones. Really sweet!
And that one over there? What's that?
That's durian.
Is durian tasty?
Really tasty, but smelly!

blocks.p: English has “this” and “that”. Bisaya has **three**, by distance: {{kini}} is near me, {{kana}} is near you, {{kadto}} is over there, away from us both. That's why you say {{Unsa kana?}} about the fruit by the vendor, and the vendor answers {{Lanzones kini}}: it's near *them*.

They work like {{siya}} in the earlier lessons: what it is comes first, then the pointing word. {{Lanzones kini}} “these are lanzones”, {{Mahal kana}} “that's expensive”. In speech you'll hear the short ones all the time: {{Unsa ni?}} “What's this?”, {{Lami kaayo ni!}} “This is really tasty!”
**{{Mao ni…}} “This is…”** introduces a person or shows the one you mean: {{Mao ni si Ben.}} “This is Ben.” And {{Mao na!}} on its own means “That's it! That's right!”

blocks.tip: In Cebu you'll also hear {{kani}} for {{kini}}: {{Unsa kani?}} Both are right.

mistakes.why: What it is comes first, then {{kini}}: the same order as {{Maestra ko}}.
About the thing in your friend’s hand, near the person you’re talking to: {{kana}}. {{kini}} is near you.

lessons.title: Introduce your family
lessons.summary: Show a photo and say “This is my mom, my dad and my sister”: my, your, his, her, our, their.
lessons.topic: {{akong}}, {{imong}}, {{iyang}}… before a noun; {{nako}}, {{nimo}}, {{niya}}… after it; {{mga}} for more than one

goal.t: Mao ni akong pamilya: akong mama, akong papa ug akong manghod.
goal.tr: This is my family: my mom, my dad and my little sister.

dialog.tr: So who are these people?

dialog.t: Akong pamilya. Mao ni akong mama ug akong papa.
dialog.tr: My family. This is my mom and my dad.
And this one? Your sister?

dialog.t: Oo, akong manghod, si Lisa. Estudyante siya.
dialog.tr: Yes, my little sister, Lisa. She's a student.
Your sister is really pretty!

dialog.t: Salamat! Ug mao ni ang among iro, si Max.
dialog.tr: Thanks! And this is our dog, Max.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: mom, house, Cebu.

blocks.p: **My, your, his…** Bisaya has two ways to say whose something is. The first goes **before** the noun and ends in -ng: {{akong mama}} “my mom”, {{imong ngalan}} “your name”. The second goes **after** the noun: {{ang mama nako}}, {{ang ngalan nimo}}. Both mean the same. Before the noun is the one you'll say most, and it often drops {{ang}}: {{Unsa imong ngalan?}}

**{{mga}} for more than one.** Bisaya nouns don't change for the plural; put {{mga}} (said “ma-NGA”) in front instead: {{akong igsoon}} “my brother or sister”, {{akong mga igsoon}} “my brothers and sisters”.

**Family words**: {{mama}}, {{papa}}, {{igsoon}} (brother or sister), {{manghod}} (younger brother or sister), {{magulang}} (older brother or sister), {{anak}} (son or daughter), {{bana}} (husband), {{asawa}} (wife), {{lolo}}, {{lola}}.

ex.t: Taga-Bohol ang akong mga lolo ug lola.

blocks.tip: Two words for “our” again: {{atong}} includes the person you're talking to, {{among}} doesn't. To your brother: {{atong balay}}. To a visitor: {{among balay}}.

mistakes.why: “My” before a noun is {{akong}}, with -ng.
{{nako}} goes after the noun. Before it, say {{akong balay}}.

practice.q: You show your house to a visitor: “This is our house.”
practice.why: The visitor doesn't live there: {{among}}, our but not yours.

practice.q: Your turn: introduce two people in your family and say one thing about each.

answers.tr: This is my dad. He's a doctor.

answers.t: Akong manghod si Sarah. Estudyante siya sa Boston.
answers.tr: Sarah is my little sister. She's a student in Boston.

lessons.title: Ask if there is one, and say what you have
lessons.summary: Ask “Is there a store near here?” and say what you have and don't have.
lessons.topic: {{naa}}, {{may}}, {{aduna}} “there is, have”; {{wala}} “there isn't, don't have”; the joining {{-y}} ({{Naa koy…}}, {{Naa bay…?}})

goal.t: Naa bay tindahan duol dinhi?
goal.tr: Is there a store near here?

dialog.t: Nang, naa bay tindahan duol dinhi?
dialog.tr: Ma'am, is there a store near here?
Yes, there's a store on the corner.
Is there an ATM?

dialog.t: Wala. Walay ATM dinhi. Naa sa mall.
dialog.tr: No. There's no ATM here. There's one at the mall.
Thanks, Ma'am!
You're welcome.

blocks.p: **There is.** {{naa}} means “there is” or “there are”. To join it to the thing, add **-y** to the end: {{Naay tindahan.}} “There's a store.” In a question, {{ba}} comes in and takes the -y: {{Naa bay tindahan?}} “Is there a store?”

**There isn't.** {{wala}} is “there isn't, there's no”, and it takes the same -y: {{Walay ATM.}} “There's no ATM.” Remember {{dili}} from the last unit? That one is for what something *is*; {{wala}} is for whether there is any.
**Have.** Bisaya says “I have” the same way: “there is, I, money”. The -y goes on the person: {{Naa koy kwarta.}} “I have money.” {{Wala koy kwarta.}} “I don't have any money.”

table: {{Naa koy iro.}} I have a dog.
{{Wala koy iro.}} I don't have a dog.
{{Naa kay iro.}} You have a dog.
{{Wala kay iro.}} You don't have a dog.
{{Naa siyay iro.}} She has a dog.
{{Wala siyay iro.}} She doesn't have a dog.

blocks.p: **Short answers.** To {{Naa bay…?}} just answer {{Naa.}} “There is.” or {{Wala.}} “There isn't.”

ex.tr: Do you have a boyfriend? / Do you have a girlfriend?
Is there a store near here?
ex.note: {{aduna}} is the same as {{naa}}, a little more careful

blocks.tip: {{naa}}, {{may}} and {{aduna}} all mean “there is”. In everyday Cebu talk {{naa}} is the one you'll hear most; {{may}} comes before the thing without -y ({{May tawo}}), and {{aduna}} is common in writing.

mistakes.tr: Is there a store near here?
mistakes.why: Join {{naa}} to the thing with -y; in a question the -y goes on {{ba}}: {{naa bay}}.
“Don't have” and “there isn't” are always {{wala}}, never {{dili}}.

practice.q: Which one means “I don't have any money”?

practice.why: In a question, {{ba}} takes the -y: {{naa bay}}.

lessons.title: Say where things and people are
lessons.summary: Say where you are, find the bathroom, and say what's on, under or next to what.
lessons.topic: {{naa}} + {{sa}} “is at”; {{wala}} “isn't here”; {{dinhi}}, {{diha}}, {{didto}}; {{sa tuo}}, {{sa wala}} and other places

goal.t: Asa man ang banyo? — Naa sa tuo.
goal.tr: Where's the bathroom? — It's on the right.

dialog.tr: Ben, are you home?

dialog.t: Wala, Ma. Naa ko sa eskwelahan.
dialog.tr: No, Mom. I'm at school.
Where are the car keys?
On the table, in the kitchen.
They're not here!

dialog.t: Ay, naa diay sa akong bag. Sorry, Ma!
dialog.tr: Oh, they're in my bag after all. Sorry, Mom!

blocks.p: **Is at.** The {{naa}} of “there is” also says where something or someone **is**: {{naa}} + {{sa}} + the place. {{Naa ko sa balay.}} “I'm at home.” One little word, {{sa}}, does the work of English “at”, “in” and “on”: {{sa balay}} at home, {{sa kusina}} in the kitchen, {{sa lamesa}} on the table.
**{{sa}} is a marker too**, like {{ang}} and {{si}}: it marks a place (and, later, a few other jobs). {{Asa}} “where” asks for it: {{Asa ka?}} “Where are you?” — {{Naa ko sa trabaho.}} “I'm at work.”
**Isn't here.** When someone or something is not at a place, Bisaya says {{wala}}, the same word as “there isn't”: {{Wala siya sa balay.}} “He's not home.” {{Wala man dinhi!}} “It's not here!”
**Here and there** match {{kini}}, {{kana}}, {{kadto}}: {{dinhi}} here (near me; {{diri}} in speech), {{diha}} there (near you), {{didto}} over there (away from us both).

table: on the right / on the left

ex.tr: The bathroom is on the left.
ex.note: {{wala}} also means “left”: the sentence tells you which

blocks.tip: {{duol}} is near, {{layo}} is far: {{Duol ra.}} “It's just nearby.” {{Layo pa.}} “It's still far.”

mistakes.why: Not at a place is {{wala}}, not {{dili}}.
A place needs {{sa}} in front of it.

lessons.title: Order food and drinks
lessons.summary: Order at a café or a carinderia: “One coffee and two ensaymadas, please.”
lessons.topic: {{gusto}} + {{og}} “a, some”; {{palihug}}; numbers with {{ka}} ({{usa ka}}, {{duha ka}}); {{lang}}

goal.t: Usa ka kape ug duha ka ensaymada, palihug.
goal.tr: One coffee and two ensaymadas, please.

dialog.t: Maayong buntag! Unsa man ang imong order, Sir?
dialog.tr: Good morning! What would you like, Sir?
I'd like a coffee, please.
Hot or iced?
Iced. And two ensaymadas.
Is that all?
Yes, that's all. Thanks!

blocks.p: **Saying what you want.** {{gusto}} is “want” or “would like”: {{Gusto ko og kape.}} “I'd like a coffee”, word for word “want I a coffee”. Before the thing you want goes {{og}}, a marker meaning “a” or “some”: {{og kape}}, {{og tubig}}.

**{{og}} is for a thing someone wants, buys, eats or drinks**, when it is not the topic of the sentence: {{og kape}}, {{og pan}}. Then the topic markers {{ang}} and {{si}}, and the place marker {{sa}}: that's four markers already.

**Numbers.** Put {{ka}} between the number and the thing: {{usa ka kape}} “one coffee”, {{duha ka ensaymada}} “two ensaymadas”. The thing doesn't change, and no {{mga}} is needed after a number. Ordering, you can just name it: {{Usa ka kape, palihug.}}
{{palihug}} is “please”, {{lang}} is “just”: {{Tubig lang, palihug.}} “Just water, please.” And {{Mao ra.}} “That's all.”

blocks.tip: {{og}} “a, some” and {{ug}} “and” sound almost the same, and many people write both as {{ug}}. This course writes {{og}} for “a, some” and {{ug}} for “and”, as the Basics course does: {{kape ug pan}}, {{Gusto ko og pan.}}

mistakes.why: The thing you want has {{og}} in front of it.
Between a number and the thing: {{ka}}.
After a number, no {{mga}}: the number already says there's more than one.

lessons.title: Ask the price and count
lessons.summary: Ask how much things cost, understand the answer, and bargain a little at the market.
lessons.topic: {{pila}} “how much, how many”; Spanish numbers for money and time; {{mga}} “about”; {{mahal}}, {{barato}}

goal.t: Pila ni? — Singkwenta pesos.
goal.tr: How much is this? — Fifty pesos.

dialog.tr: Ma'am, how much are the mangoes?
Sixty a kilo.
That's expensive! How about fifty?
Okay, fifty. How many kilos?
Two kilos, please.
A hundred altogether.

blocks.p: **How much, how many.** {{pila}} asks both. {{Pila ni?}} “How much is this?” With a thing to count, it works like a number, with {{ka}}: {{Pila ka kilo?}} “How many kilos?” {{Pila ka buok?}} “How many pieces?”

**Two sets of numbers.** You count things with the Bisaya numbers of the last lesson ({{duha ka kilo}}), but prices and the time are usually said with **Spanish** numbers: {{singkwenta pesos}} “fifty pesos”, {{alas tres}} “three o'clock”. Spanish numbers go straight before the word, with no {{ka}}.

**About.** {{mga}} before a number means “about, around”: {{mga tulo ka kilo}} “about three kilos”, {{mga alas tres}} “around three o'clock”. (It's the same {{mga}} that makes nouns plural: one word, two jobs.)

ex.t: Pila ka buok? — Lima ka buok.

ex.tr: That's really expensive! Can you give me a discount?

blocks.tip: English numbers are common in Cebu too, especially for big prices (“one fifty”), and you'll understand any of the three. When in doubt, say the price back in English: everyone will follow.

mistakes.why: {{pila}} + {{ka}} + the thing, just like a number.
Spanish numbers go straight before the word; {{ka}} is for Bisaya numbers ({{lima ka kilo}}).

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{Pila ang usa ka kilo?}} “How much is one kilo?”
A Bisaya number needs {{ka}}: {{duha ka kilo}}.

practice.q: Your turn: ask the price of something, then ask for a discount or say how many you want.

answers.tr: How much is this? That's really expensive! Can you give me a discount?

answers.t: Nang, pila ang saging? Duha ka kilo, palihug.

lessons.title: Describe what you want
lessons.summary: Say “cold water”, “a big house”, “this new phone”: join a describing word to a noun.
lessons.topic: The linker {{nga}} and its short form {{-ng}} ({{bugnaw nga tubig}}, {{dakong balay}}, {{maayong buntag}}); {{kini nga…}}

goal.t: Gusto ko og bugnaw nga tubig.
goal.tr: I'd like some cold water.

dialog.tr: What are you looking for, Ma'am?

dialog.t: Gusto ko og puti nga sinina.
dialog.tr: I'd like a white top.
This one, Ma'am? It's a new style.

dialog.t: Nindot! Pero gamay ra. Naa bay dako nga sukod?
dialog.tr: Nice! But it's too small. Is there a large size?
There is, Ma'am. Here it is.

blocks.p: In English, “cold” just sits before “water”. In Bisaya the describing word and the noun are **joined by {{nga}}**: {{bugnaw nga tubig}} “cold water”, {{puti nga sinina}} “a white top”, {{nindot nga dapit}} “a nice place”.

blocks.means: a little word that joins a describing word to the noun it describes: {{nga}}, or its short form {{-ng}}.

blocks.p: **The short form {{-ng}}.** When the first word ends in a vowel, {{nga}} usually shrinks to **-ng** on its end: {{dako nga balay}} → {{dakong balay}} “a big house”, {{bag-o nga estilo}} → {{bag-ong estilo}} “a new style”. Words ending in -n swap it for -ng: {{daghan}} → {{daghang tawo}} “many people”. Now you can see why it's {{maayong buntag}}: {{maayo}} “good” + -ng + {{buntag}} “morning”.

The pointing words join the same way: {{kini nga libro}} or {{kining libro}} “this book”, {{kanang babaye}} “that woman”. And the order can flip with no change in meaning: {{tubig nga bugnaw}} is also “cold water”, but the describing word first is more common.

ex.t: Gusto ko og init nga kape.

blocks.tip: Colors: {{puti}} white, {{itom}} black, {{pula}} red, {{asul}} blue, {{dalag}} yellow, {{berde}} green. Sizes: {{dako}} big, {{gamay}} small.

mistakes.why: Join the describing word and the noun with {{nga}}.
After a vowel, {{nga}} shrinks to -ng: {{dakong}}. (Or keep it whole: {{dako nga balay}}.)

options: {{maayo}} ends in a vowel, so {{nga}} becomes -ng
practice.why: {{maayo nga buntag}} → {{maayong buntag}}: the linker in its short form.

practice.q: In a shop: choose your replies.

lines.tr: What are you looking for, Sir?

options: Gusto ko og itom nga sapatos.
lines.why: {{itom}} ends in -m: join it with the whole {{nga}}.

answers.tr: I'd like a cold beer.

answers.t: Gusto ko og bag-ong selpon.
answers.tr: I'd like a new phone.

answers.tr: I'd like a big house near the sea.

lessons.title: Say what you want to do
lessons.summary: Say what you want (and don't want) to do: “I want to go to Bohol.”
lessons.topic: {{gusto}} + a verb with {{mo-}}; who wants: {{ko}}, {{nimo}}, {{niya}}…; {{dili}} + {{gusto}}

goal.t: Gusto ko moadto sa Bohol.
goal.tr: I want to go to Bohol.

dialog.tr: Ben, what are your plans for tomorrow?

dialog.t: Gusto ko moadto sa Bohol. Gusto nimo mouban?
dialog.tr: I want to go to Bohol. Do you want to come along?

dialog.t: Gusto ko! Gusto ko molangoy sa Panglao.
dialog.tr: I'd love to! I want to swim at Panglao.

dialog.t: Ug gusto ko motan-aw sa Chocolate Hills.
dialog.tr: And I want to see the Chocolate Hills.

dialog.t: Pero dili ko gusto mosakay og barko. Kusog ang balod!
dialog.tr: But I don't want to take the boat. The waves are big!

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: go, eat, swim, want.

blocks.p: **Gusto + a verb.** To say what you want to do, put the verb after {{gusto}} and give it **mo-** on the front: {{adto}} “go” → {{Gusto ko moadto.}} “I want to go.” {{kaon}} “eat” → {{Gusto ko mokaon.}} “I want to eat.”

blocks.means: the bare core of a word, the form a dictionary lists: {{kaon}} (eat), {{adto}} (go). Bisaya builds verbs by adding pieces to the root.

blocks.p: {{mo-}} is the form of a verb for something **not done yet**. You'll meet it again and again; for now, it's the form that follows {{gusto}}: {{molangoy}} “to swim”, {{mopalit}} “to buy”, {{motan-aw}} “to see, to watch”.

**Who wants.** After {{gusto}}, “I” is {{ko}} (or {{nako}}), but the others come from the set you know for “my, your” after a noun: {{gusto nimo}} (short {{mo}}), {{gusto niya}}. So {{Gusto nimo mouban?}} “Do you want to come along?” and {{Gusto niya molangoy.}} “She wants to swim.”
**Don't want.** {{dili}} goes in front, and the short word follows it: {{Dili ko gusto mosakay og barko.}} “I don't want to take the boat.”

ex.tr: Do you want to come along?
I don't want to work today.
Where do you want to eat?

blocks.tip: You'll also hear {{gusto kong moadto}}, with -ng joining {{ko}} to the verb. It means exactly the same.

mistakes.tr: I want to go to Bohol.
mistakes.why: The verb after {{gusto}} takes {{mo-}}.
After {{gusto}}, he or she is {{niya}}, the word for “his, her” after a noun.

practice.tr: I want to go to Bohol.
I don't want to work today.

practice.q: Your friend has an idea for the weekend. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Do you want to go to Moalboal?

lines.t: Ug gusto nimo mokaon og lechon?
lines.tr: And do you want to eat lechon?

options: Dili ko gusto. Busog pa ko.

practice.q: Say “I want to buy a new phone.”
practice.answer: Gusto ko mopalit og bag-ong selpon.

practice.why: The short word goes right after {{dili}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you want to do this year, and one you don't.

answers.t: Gusto ko moadto sa Siargao. Gusto ko mokat-on og Bisaya.
answers.tr: I want to go to Siargao. I want to learn Bisaya.

answers.t: Gusto ko molangoy sa dagat. Dili ko gusto mosakay og eroplano.
answers.tr: I want to swim in the sea. I don't want to take a plane.

answers.t: Gusto ko mopalit og bag-ong awto. Dili ko gusto motrabaho matag Sabado.
answers.tr: I want to buy a new car. I don't want to work every Saturday.

lessons.title: Say what you're going to do
lessons.summary: Talk about tomorrow, tonight and next week: “I'm going to the market tomorrow.”
lessons.topic: {{mo-}} for what is still to come; {{ugma}}, {{unya}}, {{karong gabii}}; {{dili}} + {{mo-}} “won't”

goal.t: Moadto ko sa merkado ugma.
goal.tr: I'm going to the market tomorrow.

dialog.tr: Where are you going tomorrow?

dialog.t: Moadto ko sa merkado sa buntag.
dialog.tr: I'm going to the market in the morning.
And in the afternoon?

dialog.t: Mobisita ko sa akong higala sa Mandaue.
dialog.tr: I'm visiting my friend in Mandaue.
I'll come with you to the market!
Okay! We'll leave at eight.

blocks.p: You met {{mo-}} after {{gusto}}. On its own, at the start of a sentence, it says the action is **still to come**: {{Moadto ko.}} “I'll go, I'm going (to go).” English chooses between “will” and “going to”; Bisaya {{mo-}} covers both.
**The order**: the verb first, then the short word, then the rest. {{Moadto ko sa merkado ugma.}} is “will-go I to the market tomorrow”.

blocks.means: a piece added to the front of a word to change its meaning: {{mo-}} in {{moadto}}.

blocks.p: **When.** {{ugma}} tomorrow, {{unya}} later, {{karong gabii}} tonight, {{karong hapon}} this afternoon, {{sunod semana}} next week, {{sa Lunes}} on Monday.
**Won't.** {{dili}} + the {{mo-}} verb, with the short word after {{dili}}: {{Dili ko moadto.}} “I won't go, I'm not going.”

blocks.tip: {{Mouban ko!}} “I'll come along!” is a handy one: {{uban}} is “with, together”.

mistakes.why: The verb first; {{ko}} right after it.
With {{dili}} first, {{ko}} follows {{dili}}.

lines.tr: Where are you going this afternoon?

lines.why: {{ta}} “we” is a short word too: after the verb.

practice.q: Your turn: say two or three things you'll do tomorrow, and one you won't.

answers.t: Moadto ko sa trabaho. Mokaon ko sa gawas. Dili ko mouli og sayo.
answers.tr: I'll go to work. I'll eat out. I won't go home early.

answers.t: Mobisita ko sa akong lola ugma. Dili ko motrabaho.
answers.tr: I'm visiting my grandma tomorrow. I won't work.

lessons.title: Describe your day
lessons.summary: Say what you do every day and when: “I get up at six every morning.”
lessons.topic: {{mo-}} for habits; telling the time with {{alas}}; {{matag}}, {{kanunay}}, {{usahay}}; the time first, then the short word

goal.t: Alas sais ko mobangon matag buntag.
goal.tr: I get up at six every morning.

dialog.tr: What time do you get up?

dialog.t: Alas sais ko mobangon. Dayon moinom ko og kape.
dialog.tr: I get up at six. Then I drink coffee.
Always?
Yes, every day! And you?

dialog.t: Alas nuwebe. Dili ko moinom og kape, tsaa lang.
dialog.tr: Nine. I don't drink coffee, just tea.
Nine? Lucky you!

blocks.p: **{{mo-}} for habits.** The {{mo-}} of the last lesson also says what you do **regularly**: {{Mobangon ko alas sais.}} “I get up at six.” {{mo-}} means “not one finished event”: something still to come, or something that keeps coming back. Words like {{matag adlaw}} “every day” make it clear.

**The time.** {{alas}} + a Spanish number: {{alas sais}} “six o'clock”, {{alas dose}} “twelve”, {{alas siyete y medya}} “half past seven”. {{Unsang orasa?}} is “What time?” (word for word “what-hour”, with -ng joining {{unsa}} to {{orasa}}). Parts of the day: {{sa buntag}} in the morning, {{sa udto}} at noon, {{sa hapon}} in the afternoon, {{sa gabii}} in the evening.
**The time can come first**, and then, as always, the short word follows the first word: {{Alas sais ko mobangon.}} “At six I get up.” You can also say {{Mobangon ko alas sais.}}: both are natural.

ex.t: Moinom ko og kape matag buntag.
Alas siyete ko mosulod sa trabaho.

blocks.tip: Days of the week, from Spanish: {{Lunes}}, {{Martes}}, {{Miyerkules}}, {{Huwebes}}, {{Biyernes}}, {{Sabado}}, {{Domingo}}.

mistakes.why: When the time comes first, {{ko}} goes right after it. (Or start with the verb: {{Mobangon ko alas sais.}})

mistakes.tr: What time do you get up?
mistakes.why: {{unsa}} joins {{orasa}} with -ng: {{unsang orasa}}.

practice.q: A new coworker asks about your day. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What time do you get up?

lines.t: Sayo kaayo! Moinom ka og kape?
lines.tr: That's really early! Do you drink coffee?

practice.q: {{Moadto ko sa simbahan matag Domingo.}} is about…
Your turn: describe your morning: when you get up and what you do.

answers.t: Alas siyete ko mobangon. Moinom ko og kape, dayon moadto ko sa trabaho.
answers.tr: I get up at seven. I drink coffee, then I go to work.

answers.t: Alas singko ko mobangon matag adlaw. Usahay modagan ko sa parke.
answers.tr: I get up at five every day. Sometimes I run in the park.

lessons.title: Say what you're doing, and where you live and work
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing right now, and where you live and work: “I work at a hotel, and I'm studying Bisaya.”
lessons.topic: {{nag-}} for an action going on; {{Nag-unsa ka?}} “What are you doing?”; {{ga-}} in Cebu speech

goal.t: Nagtrabaho ko sa usa ka hotel, ug nagtuon ko og Bisaya.
goal.tr: I work at a hotel, and I'm studying Bisaya.

dialog.tr: Where do you live, Ben?
I live in Lahug. And you?
In Mandaue. Where do you work?

dialog.t: Nagtrabaho ko sa usa ka hotel. Ug nagtuon ko og Bisaya!
dialog.tr: I work at a hotel. And I'm studying Bisaya!
Great! How's it going?
It's hard, but I'm enjoying it.

blocks.p: **{{nag-}}: going on.** {{nag-}} on the front of a verb says the action **is going on**: right now ({{Nagluto ko.}} “I'm cooking.”) or for a stretch of time, like a job or a home ({{Nagtrabaho ko sa hotel.}} “I work at a hotel.” {{Nagpuyo ko sa Lahug.}} “I live in Lahug.”).

**Now or then?** Bisaya doesn't say. {{Nagluto ko}} can also be “I was cooking” or “I cooked”; words like {{karon}} “now” or {{gahapon}} “yesterday” tell you when. What {{nag-}} says is that the action went on for a while.
**“What are you doing?”** is {{Nag-unsa ka?}}, word for word “doing-what you?”: {{nag-}} works even on {{unsa}} “what”. It's one of the commonest questions in Cebu, on the phone and in the street.

ex.t: Nagdula ang mga bata sa gawas.

blocks.tip: In Cebu City you'll hear **ga-** for things happening right now: {{Gaunsa ka?}} “What are you doing?”, {{Gakaon ko.}} “I'm eating.” It means the same as {{nag-}} here; this course writes {{nag-}}.

mistakes.why: After the first word, use the short {{ka}}.
A place needs {{sa}}.

practice.why: {{nag-}} says the action went on, not when.
A job that's going on: {{nag-}}. ({{Motrabaho}} would be “I'll work”.)

practice.q: Your friend calls. Choose your replies.
Which one is a daily habit?
practice.why: {{mo-}} for what you do regularly; {{nag-}} + {{karon}} for right now.

practice.q: Say “Mom is at home. She's cooking.”
practice.answer: Naa sa balay si Mama. Nagluto siya.

practice.q: Your turn: where do you live and work, and what are you doing right now?

answers.t: Nagpuyo ko sa Seattle. Nagtrabaho ko sa usa ka opisina. Karon, nagtuon ko og Bisaya!
answers.tr: I live in Seattle. I work in an office. Right now, I'm studying Bisaya!

answers.t: Nagpuyo ko sa Cebu City. Estudyante ko. Karon, naghulat ko sa akong higala.
answers.tr: I live in Cebu City. I'm a student. Right now, I'm waiting for my friend.

lessons.title: Tell what you did
lessons.summary: Say what you did yesterday and answer Cebu's favorite question, “Have you eaten?”
lessons.topic: {{mi-}} (in speech also {{ni-}}) for a finished action; {{gahapon}}, {{ganiha}}; {{na}} “already”

goal.t: Miadto ko sa baybayon gahapon.
goal.tr: I went to the beach yesterday.

dialog.tr: Have you eaten?
Yes, I've eaten. You?

dialog.t: Nikaon na sad ko. Unsay imong gibuhat gahapon?
dialog.tr: I've eaten too. What did you do yesterday?

dialog.t: Miadto ko sa baybayon. Milangoy ko, ug mikaon mi og sugba.
dialog.tr: I went to the beach. I swam, and we ate grilled fish.
Who were you with?

dialog.t: Akong mga higala. Miuli mi alas siyete sa gabii.
dialog.tr: My friends. We came home at seven in the evening.

blocks.p: **{{mi-}}: done.** {{mo-}} is for what's still to come; {{mi-}} is for what **happened**: {{Moadto ko.}} “I'll go.” → {{Miadto ko.}} “I went.” One letter changes, and the rest of the sentence stays the same.

**{{ni-}} is the same as {{mi-}}.** In Cebu conversation you'll hear {{ni-}} all the time ({{Nikaon ka na?}} {{Niadto ko.}}). Both are right; this course writes {{mi-}}, as the Basics course does, and lets people in the conversations say {{ni-}}.

**{{na}} “already, now”.** {{Mikaon na ko.}} is “I've already eaten.” So {{Nikaon ka na?}}, word for word “ate you already?”, is “Have you eaten?”: in Cebu it's also a friendly “How are you?”. English chooses between “I ate” and “I've eaten”; Bisaya uses {{mi-}} for both.
**When**: {{gahapon}} yesterday, {{ganiha}} earlier today, {{niadtong Lunes}} last Monday, {{sa miaging semana}} last week.

blocks.tip: {{Unsay imong gibuhat?}} “What did you do?” uses a different kind of verb ({{gi-}}), coming in unit 4. You can already use it as a whole phrase.

mistakes.tr: I went to the beach yesterday.
mistakes.why: Yesterday is done: {{mi-}}. {{mo-}} is for what's still to come.

practice.tr: I went to the beach yesterday.

practice.why: {{ni-}} is the same as {{mi-}}: done; {{na}} is “already”.

practice.q: Monday morning at work: choose your replies.

practice.why: {{mo-}} is for what's still to come; yesterday is done.

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you did yesterday.

answers.t: Miadto ko sa trabaho. Mikaon ko sa gawas. Miuli ko alas siyete.
answers.tr: I went to work. I ate out. I went home at seven.

answers.t: Milangoy ko sa dagat ug mipalit ko og sugba.
answers.tr: I swam in the sea and I bought some grilled fish.

lessons.title: Say what you didn't do, and what you haven't done yet
lessons.summary: Say “I didn't go”, “I haven't eaten yet” and “not anymore”.
lessons.topic: {{wala}} + {{mo-}} “didn't”; {{wala pa}} “not yet”; {{na}} and {{pa}}

goal.t: Wala pa ko mokaon. Ikaw, nikaon ka na?
goal.tr: I haven't eaten yet. And you, have you eaten?

dialog.tr: Ben, have you eaten?
Not yet, Mom.

dialog.t: Mitawag ka na sa imong lola?
dialog.tr: Have you called your grandma?

dialog.t: Wala pa ko motawag. Ugma na lang.
dialog.tr: I haven't called yet. I'll do it tomorrow.

dialog.t: Ug ganiha, nganong wala ka moadto sa eskwelahan?
dialog.tr: And earlier, why didn't you go to school?

dialog.t: Miadto ko, Ma! Wala lang ko mosulod sa klase…
dialog.tr: I did go, Mom! I just didn't go into class…

blocks.p: **Didn't.** For something that didn't happen, use {{wala}}, and the verb goes **back to {{mo-}}**: {{Miadto ko.}} “I went.” → {{Wala ko moadto.}} “I didn't go.” It looks odd at first, but it's simple: after {{wala}}, always {{mo-}}.
**Not yet.** {{wala pa}} + {{mo-}}: {{Wala pa ko mokaon.}} “I haven't eaten yet.” The short answer is just {{Wala pa.}} “Not yet.”
**{{na}} and {{pa}}** are a pair. {{na}} is “already, now, anymore”; {{pa}} is “still, yet”. {{Naa pa siya.}} “He's still here.” {{Wala na siya.}} “He's gone, he's not here anymore.”

table: {{Wala pa ko mokaon.}} I haven't eaten yet.

ex.tr: I didn't go because it was raining.

blocks.tip: In fast speech you'll also hear {{wala}} with {{mi-}} or {{ni-}} ({{Wala siya mitubag.}} “She didn't answer.”). People understand both; {{wala}} + {{mo-}} is the standard you can always use.

mistakes.why: “Didn't” is {{wala}}. {{Dili ko moadto}} is “I won't go”.
“Not yet” is {{wala pa}}; {{wala na}} is “not anymore”.

practice.q: Your friend checks on you. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Ha? Alas tres na! Nganong wala ka mokaon?
lines.tr: What? It's three o'clock! Why haven't you eaten?

options: Busy kaayo ko. Wala koy oras.
Busy kaayo ko. Dili koy oras.
lines.why: No time: {{wala koy oras}}, like “I have no money”.

practice.q: Answer: {{Miadto ka sa baybayon?}} “No, I didn't go.”
Your turn: say one thing you've already done today and one you haven't done yet.

lessons.title: Ask about someone's day
lessons.summary: Ask when, why, what time and who: “When did you arrive? Why didn't you call?”
lessons.topic: Question word + short word + verb; {{kanus-a}}, {{nganong}}, {{unsang orasa}}, {{kinsa ang}}

goal.t: Kanus-a ka miabot? Nganong wala ka motawag?
goal.tr: When did you arrive? Why didn't you call?

dialog.tr: Ben! When did you arrive?
Yesterday already.

dialog.t: Gahapon pa? Nganong wala ka motawag?
dialog.tr: Yesterday? Why didn't you call?

dialog.t: Gikapoy kaayo ko. Natulog ko dayon.
dialog.tr: I was really tired. I went straight to sleep.
Where are you staying now?

dialog.t: Sa usa ka hotel duol sa Colon.
dialog.tr: At a hotel near Colon Street.

dialog.t: Unsang orasa ka mahuman sa trabaho? Kaon ta!
dialog.tr: What time do you finish work? Let's eat!

blocks.p: You know the pattern from the first unit: **the question word first, the short word right after it**. Now a verb follows: {{Asa ka moadto?}} “Where are you going?”, {{Kanus-a ka miabot?}} “When did you arrive?”

**The verb keeps its own form**: {{mo-}} for what's still to come ({{Kanus-a ka mobalik?}} “When will you come back?”), {{mi-}} for what happened ({{Kanus-a ka miabot?}}), {{nag-}} for what's going on ({{Asa ka nagtrabaho?}} “Where do you work?”), and {{wala}} + {{mo-}} for what didn't.

table: {{Kanus-a ka mobalik?}} When will you come back?
{{Nganong wala ka moabot?}} Why didn't you come?
{{Unsang orasa ka mobiya?}} What time are you leaving?
{{Pila ka tawo ang miadto?}} How many people went?

blocks.p: **Two details.** {{ngano}} “why” usually joins the rest with -ng: {{Nganong…?}} (alone: {{Ngano man?}} “Why?”). And to ask **who did** something, put {{ang}} after {{kinsa}}: {{Kinsa ang nitawag?}}, often said {{Kinsay nitawag?}}

blocks.tip: {{Asa ka paingon?}} “Where are you headed?” is how people greet each other in the street. A vague answer is fine: {{Diha lang.}} “Just over there.”

mistakes.why: {{ka}} comes right after the question word, before the verb.
Same rule: the short word follows the first word.

lines.t: Ganiha lang. Gikan ko sa Siargao.
lines.tr: Just earlier. I've come from Siargao.

answers.t: Unsang orasa ka mibangon? Asa ka miadto? Kinsa imong kauban?
answers.tr: What time did you get up? Where did you go? Who were you with?

answers.t: Kanus-a ka miuli? Nikaon ka na?
answers.tr: When did you get home? Have you eaten?

lessons.title: Tell people what to do, nicely
lessons.summary: Invite a guest to sit and eat, say “Let's go!”, and “Don't worry.”
lessons.topic: The root as a command; {{palihug}} and {{sa}}; {{ta}} “let's”; {{ayaw}} “don't”

goal.t: Lingkod, palihug. Kaon na ta!
goal.tr: Have a seat, please. Let's eat!

dialog.tr: Come in, come in! Have a seat, please.
Thank you, Lola.

dialog.t: Kaon na ta! Kuha og kan-on.
dialog.tr: Let's eat! Take some rice.
This is really delicious, Lola!
Eat some more! There's plenty.

dialog.t: Busog na kaayo ko, Lola. Salamat kaayo!
dialog.tr: I'm really full, Lola. Thank you so much!
Wait, there's still dessert!

blocks.p: **The bare root is a command.** No {{mo-}}, no ending: {{Lingkod!}} “Sit down!”, {{Kaon!}} “Eat!”, {{Hulat!}} “Wait!”, {{Dali!}} “Hurry!”. With a thing, add {{og}}: {{Kuha og kan-on.}} “Take some rice.”

**Make it gentle.** Add {{palihug}} “please”, before or after: {{Lingkod, palihug.}} And {{sa}} after the command means “first, for a moment”: {{Hulat sa.}} “Wait a moment.” (It's not the place marker {{sa}}: same sound, different job.)
**Let's.** The root + {{ta}}, the short “we (you and I)”: {{Kaon ta!}} “Let's eat!”, {{Adto ta!}} “Let's go!”, {{Kaon na ta!}} “Let's eat now!”

**Don't.** {{ayaw}}, usually with {{og}}: {{Ayaw og saba!}} “Don't be noisy!” Some phrases have their own shape, like {{Ayaw kabalaka.}} “Don't worry.” That makes three words for “no”: {{dili}} (is not, won't), {{wala}} (there isn't, didn't), {{ayaw}} (don't!).

blocks.tip: Unit 4 adds a second kind of command, for one particular thing: {{Kuhaa ang tubig!}} “Get the water!” For now, the bare root does almost everything.

mistakes.why: Telling someone not to do something: {{ayaw}}.
{{ta}} is a short word: after the verb.

lessons.title: Ask the way and give directions
lessons.summary: Ask how to get somewhere, follow the answer, and tell a jeepney driver where to stop.
lessons.topic: {{Unsaon pag-adto sa…?}}; directions as commands: {{diretso}}, {{liko}}, {{sakay}}, {{naog}}; {{sa tuo}}, {{sa wala}}

goal.t: Unsaon pag-adto sa Basilica? — Diretso lang, dayon liko sa wala.
goal.tr: How do I get to the Basilica? — Just go straight, then turn left.

dialog.t: Nong, palihug, unsaon pag-adto sa Basilica?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, sir, how do I get to the Basilica?

dialog.t: Diretso lang, dayon liko sa wala sa ikaduhang kanto.
dialog.tr: Just go straight, then turn left at the second corner.
Is it still far?

dialog.t: Dili, duol ra. Mga lima ka minuto.
dialog.tr: No, it's close. About five minutes.
Thank you very much, sir!
You're welcome. Take care!

blocks.p: **How do I get to…?** {{Unsaon pag-adto sa…?}}, word for word “how-to going to…?”. {{pag-}} turns a verb into an “-ing” word: {{pag-adto}} “going”. It works for any “how do you…”: {{Unsaon pagluto niini?}} “How do you cook this?”

**Directions are commands**, with the bare root from the last lesson: {{Diretso lang.}} “Just go straight.” {{Liko sa tuo.}} “Turn right.” {{Sakay og jeep.}} “Take a jeepney.” {{Naog sa simbahan.}} “Get off at the church.” And to link the steps: {{dayon}} “then”, {{human ana}} “after that”.

**First, second, third**: {{una}} (first), then {{ika-}} + the number: {{ikaduha}} second, {{ikatulo}} third. They join their noun with -ng like any describing word: {{ikaduhang kanto}} “the second corner”.

ex.tr: How do I get to Ayala?
Turn right at the traffic light.

ex.t: Sakay og jeep paingon sa Colon.

ex.tr: Get off in front of the church.

ex.note: to a jeepney or taxi driver

blocks.tip: On a jeepney, pass your fare forward with {{Palihug, plete.}} “Fare, please.” When you want to get off, call out {{Lugar lang!}}

{{tuo}} and {{wala}} are places: they need {{sa}}.

lessons.title: Say what you did with a particular thing
lessons.summary: Say “I bought the shoes” (not just “some shoes”) and ask “Where did you buy that?”
lessons.topic: Focus on the thing: {{gi-}} + the doer ({{nako}}, {{nimo}}…) + {{ang}}; {{og}} “a thing” vs {{ang}} “the thing”

goal.t: Asa nimo gipalit kana? — Gipalit nako sa Carbon.
goal.tr: Where did you buy that? — I bought it at Carbon Market.

dialog.t: Nindot kaayo ang imong bag! Asa nimo gipalit?
dialog.tr: Your bag is really nice! Where did you buy it?

dialog.t: Gipalit nako sa Carbon. Barato ra kaayo!
dialog.tr: I bought it at Carbon. It was really cheap!
What else did you buy?

dialog.t: Mipalit ko og sapatos ug duha ka sinina.
dialog.tr: I bought some shoes and two dresses.
So where are the shoes?
I left them at home.

blocks.p: Until now, the verb has always pointed at **the doer**: in {{Mipalit ko og sapatos}} “I bought some shoes”, {{ko}} is the topic. Bisaya verbs can also point at **the thing**: {{Gipalit nako ang sapatos.}} “I bought the shoes”, word for word “bought-by-me the shoes”. Now {{ang sapatos}} is the topic, and the doer moves into the {{nako}} set.

blocks.means: which part of the sentence the verb points at, the one marked {{ang}} or {{si}}. {{mi-}}, {{mo-}} and {{nag-}} verbs point at the doer; {{gi-}} points at the thing done to.

blocks.p: **When to use which?** Use {{gi-}} when the thing is **particular**: “the”, “this”, “my”, or something already talked about. Use {{mi-}} + {{og}} when it's just “a, some”. That's why Ana says {{Gipalit nako}} about the bag Joy is looking at, but {{Mipalit ko og sapatos}} about shoes not yet mentioned.

table: a thing: the doer in focus
the thing: the thing in focus
{{Mipalit ko og sapatos.}} I bought some shoes.
{{Gipalit nako ang sapatos.}} I bought the shoes.
{{Mikaon siya og mangga.}} She ate a mango.
{{Gikaon niya ang mangga.}} She ate the mango.
{{Mibasa ko og libro.}} I read a book.
{{Gibasa nako kini nga libro.}} I read this book.

blocks.p: **The doer** of a {{gi-}} verb comes from the set you know from “my, your” after a noun and from {{gusto}}: {{nako}} (short {{ko}}), {{nimo}} (short {{mo}}), {{niya}}, {{namo}}, {{nato}}, {{ninyo}}, {{nila}}. And “it” still isn't said: {{Gipalit nako.}} “I bought it.” {{Asa nimo gipalit?}} “Where did you buy it?”

ex.t: Gikaon nako ang imong cake. Sorry!
Gitan-aw namo ang sine sa Ayala.
ex.tr: We watched the movie at Ayala.

blocks.tip: {{gi-}} is the “done” form. The next lessons give it a “not yet” form and a command, just as {{mi-}} has {{mo-}}.

mistakes.why: The doer of a {{gi-}} verb is {{nako}} (or the short {{ko}}), not {{ako}}.
A {{gi-}} verb points at a particular thing, marked {{ang}}. For “some shoes”, say {{Mipalit ko og sapatos.}}
In a {{mi-}} sentence {{ang}} belongs to the doer. For “the mango”, point the verb at it: {{gi-}}.

practice.why: Particular shoes: the verb points at them with {{gi-}}.

lines.why: The phone you're both looking at: {{gipalit nako}}, “I bought it”.
Something new to the conversation, “a case”: {{mi-}} + {{og}}.

practice.why: Both are done; {{og}} is “a”, {{ang}} with {{gi-}} is “the”.

lessons.title: Tell who did what
lessons.summary: Say “The dog ate the fish!” and “Mom cooked the adobo”, and ask who did it.
lessons.topic: The doer of a {{gi-}} verb: {{ni}} + a name, {{sa}} + a noun; {{ni}} and {{sa}} for “of”; all the markers together

goal.t: Gikaon sa iro ang isda!
goal.tr: The dog ate the fish!

dialog.t: Asa man ang isda? Giluto nako ganiha!
dialog.tr: Where's the fish? I cooked it earlier!
The dog ate it, Mom!
What? And the cake?
Lisa ate it.

dialog.t: Dili tinuod! Gikaon ni Ben ang katunga!
dialog.tr: Not true! Ben ate half!

dialog.t: Hala! Kinsa man ang mohugas sa mga plato?
dialog.tr: Oh no! So who's going to wash the dishes?
Ben!

blocks.p: In the last lesson the doer of a {{gi-}} verb was a pronoun ({{nako}}, {{niya}}). When the doer is a **name**, it takes {{ni}}: {{Gikaon ni Lisa ang cake.}} “Lisa ate the cake.” When it's an ordinary **noun**, it takes {{sa}}: {{Gikaon sa iro ang isda.}} “The dog ate the fish.”

So {{sa}}, the place marker, has a second job: the doer of a {{gi-}} verb. And {{ni}} is its partner for names, just as {{si}} is {{ang}}'s partner. A sentence has **only one** {{ang}} or {{si}}: the focus.
**“Of” too.** The same {{sa}} and {{ni}} say whose something is: {{ang balay ni Lito}} “Lito's house”, {{ang ngalan sa iro}} “the dog's name”.

**Asking who did it.** After {{kinsa ang}}, Bisaya uses the doer verb ({{mi-}}, {{nag-}}): {{Kinsa ang nagluto niini?}} “Who cooked this?” {{Kinsa ang mikaon sa cake?}} “Who ate the cake?” (Here {{sa}} marks “the cake”: the doer has the {{ang}}.) Lesson 42 comes back to this.

ex.t: Gibasa sa maestra ang akong sulat.
Gipalit ni Ben ang mga tiket.
Unsa ang ngalan sa imong iro?

blocks.tip: The order after the verb is free: {{Giluto ni Mama ang adobo}} and {{Giluto ang adobo ni Mama}} mean the same. The markers, not the order, tell you who did what.

mistakes.why: The doer's name takes {{ni}}; {{si}} is for the focus.
Only one {{ang}} per sentence. The doer takes {{sa}}.

practice.q: Someone broke the vase. Choose your replies.

lines.why: Answering “who”, name the doer as the focus: {{Ang iring}} “The cat”.

options: Oo! Giduso sa iring ang plorera.
Oo! Giduso ang iring ang plorera.
lines.why: In a {{gi-}} sentence the doer takes {{sa}}; only the vase has {{ang}}.

practice.q: Which doer goes in {{Gipalit ___ ang sapatos}} “I bought the shoes”?
practice.why: A pronoun doer comes from the {{nako}} set.

practice.answer: Unsa ang ngalan sa imong iro?

practice.q: Your turn: say who did something at your home or work recently.

answers.tr: Dad cooked the main dish.

answers.t: Gikaon sa akong iring ang isda!
answers.tr: My cat ate the fish!

answers.t: Gipalit ni Lisa ang pan ganiha.
answers.tr: Lisa bought the bread earlier.

lessons.title: Say what you'll do with it, and ask someone to do it
lessons.summary: Say “I'll take this one”, “We'll watch the movie tonight”, and “Get the water, please.”
lessons.topic: {{-on}} (not yet) and {{-a}} (command) for a particular thing: {{paliton}}, {{palita}}; sound changes ({{basahon}}, {{imna}})

goal.t: Paliton nako kini. Putosa, palihug.
goal.tr: I'll take this one. Please wrap it.

dialog.tr: Look at this! Nice, isn't it?
Nice! Are you going to buy it?

dialog.t: Oo, paliton nako. Nong, pila ni?
dialog.tr: Yes, I'll buy it. Sir, how much is this?
Eight hundred, Ma'am.
Okay. Please wrap it.
Thank you, Ma'am! Come back anytime!

blocks.p: **Not yet: -on.** Just as {{mi-}} has {{mo-}}, the {{gi-}} verb has a form for what's still to come: drop {{gi-}} and add **-on** at the end. {{Gipalit nako.}} “I bought it.” → {{Paliton nako.}} “I'll buy it.” The doer and the {{ang}} thing stay exactly as they were.

**Commands: -a.** To tell someone to do something to a particular thing, add **-a**: {{Palita!}} “Buy it!”, {{Tan-awa!}} “Look at it!”, {{Kuhaa ang tubig.}} “Get the water.” Compare the bare root of lesson 19, for “some”: {{Kuha og tubig.}} “Get some water.”

**Small sound changes.** Some roots add an h before the ending ({{basa}} → {{basahon}}, {{basaha}}); some lose a vowel ({{inom}} → {{imnon}}, {{imna}}; {{dala}} “bring” → {{dad-on}}, {{dad-a}}). Learn them as you meet them, the way you'd learn “bring, brought”.

ex.t: Tan-awon nato ang sine karong gabii.

ex.tr: Get the water from the fridge.
What do I do with this?

blocks.tip: {{Unsaon}} “how, what to do with” is itself an -on form of {{unsa}}: {{Unsaon nako ni?}} “What do I do with this?”, {{Unsaon pagluto niini?}} “How do you cook this?”

mistakes.why: A particular thing ({{ang}}): the command takes -a. The bare root goes with {{og}}: {{Kuha og tubig.}}
Tomorrow is not yet: -on. {{gi-}} is for what's done.

practice.why: A command about a particular thing: -a.

practice.q: {{Kuha og tubig.}} and {{Kuhaa ang tubig.}} mean…
Shopping with a friend: choose your replies.

lines.tr: That dress is nice! Are you going to buy it?

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you'll do with particular things this week (a book, a movie, your room…).

answers.tr: I'll read the book this week.

answers.t: Tan-awon namo ang bag-ong sine sa Sabado.
answers.tr: We'll watch the new movie on Saturday.

lessons.title: Call, help and visit people
lessons.summary: Say “Call me tomorrow”, “She told me” and “I'll help you”, the Bisaya way.
lessons.topic: Focus on the person or place: {{gi-…-an}} (done), {{-an}} (not yet), {{-i}} (command); {{tika}} “I … you”

goal.t: Tawagi ko ugma. Tabangan tika.
goal.tr: Call me tomorrow. I'll help you.

dialog.t: Ben, mobalhin ko og balay sa Sabado.
dialog.tr: Ben, I'm moving house on Saturday.
I'll help you! What time?

dialog.t: Alas otso. Salamat kaayo! Gitabangan ko ni Lito sa miaging tuig, pero naa siya sa Manila karon.
dialog.tr: Eight o'clock. Thanks so much! Lito helped me last year, but he's in Manila now.

dialog.t: Walay problema. Tawagi ko sa Biyernes, ha?
dialog.tr: No problem. Call me on Friday, okay?
Okay. I'll call you.

blocks.p: Some verbs act on **a person or a place** rather than on a thing you handle: call someone, help someone, tell someone, give someone something, clean a room, open a door. These point at the person or place with **-an**: {{gi-…-an}} when it's done, {{-an}} when it's not yet, and {{-i}} for a command.

**Who's who.** The person in focus takes the topic words ({{ko}}, {{siya}}, {{ang}}, {{si}}); the doer takes the {{nako}} set, {{ni}} or {{sa}}, as in the last lessons. So {{Gitawagan ko niya.}} is “She called me” (I was the one called, she did it), and {{Gitawagan nako siya.}} is “I called her”. Watch {{ko}}: it can be the topic “I” or the short doer “by me”; its place in the sentence tells you which.

**{{tika}}: I … you.** When “I” does something to “you”, Bisaya melts {{ko}} and {{ka}} into one word, {{tika}}: {{Tawagan tika.}} “I'll call you.” {{Tabangan tika.}} “I'll help you.” And the famous one: {{Gihigugma tika.}} “I love you.”

blocks.tip: Which verbs take -an and which take -on is part of each verb, like a noun's plural in English. The commonest are in the table; the Basics course's sentences show many more.

mistakes.why: {{tawag}} points at the person with -an: its command is {{tawagi}}.
“I … you” melts into {{tika}}.

practice.q: Your friend needs a hand. Choose your replies.

lines.why: You're offering: “I'll help you”, -an. ({{Tabangi}} is a command.)

practice.q: In {{Gitawagan ko niya}}, who did the calling?

practice.q: Your turn: ask a friend to call or help you, and offer to do something for them.

answers.t: Tawagi ko sa Sabado. Tabangan tika sa imong proyekto.
answers.tr: Call me on Saturday. I'll help you with your project.

answers.tr: Please help me tomorrow. I'll call you later.

lessons.title: Give, put and send things
lessons.summary: Say “Give this to Mom”, “Put it in the fridge” and “I sent the money to Dad.”
lessons.topic: Focus on the thing that moves: {{i-}} (not yet, command), {{gi-}} (done); {{kang}} + a name; {{kanako}}, {{kanimo}}… “to me, to you”

goal.t: Ihatag ni kang Mama, palihug.
goal.tr: Please give this to Mom.

dialog.t: Ben, ibutang ang mga plato sa lamesa.
dialog.tr: Ben, put the plates on the table.
Where should I put the cake?

dialog.t: Ibutang sa ref. Ug kini nga sulat, ihatag kang Lola.
dialog.tr: Put it in the fridge. And this letter, give it to Lola.

dialog.t: Ma, gihatag na nako kaniya ang usa ganiha.
dialog.tr: Mom, I already gave her one earlier.

dialog.t: Lahi kini, para sa iyang birthday. Ihatag na!
dialog.tr: This one's different, it's for her birthday. Go give it to her!

blocks.p: A third kind of focus: on the thing that **moves**: what you give, put, send, write or say. These verbs take **i-** for “not yet” and for commands ({{Ihatag ni.}} “Give this.” {{Ibutang diha.}} “Put it there.”) and {{gi-}} when done ({{Gihatag nako.}} “I gave it.”).

**To whom?** {{kang}} before a name ({{kang Mama}}, {{kang Ben}}), {{sa}} before a noun ({{sa maestra}}). For pronouns there's a third set, used after “to, for” words: {{kanako}} to me, {{kanimo}} to you, {{kaniya}} to him or her. That completes the pronouns: one set per marker.

ex.tr: Where did you put the key?

ex.t: Gipadala nako ang kwarta kang Papa.
ex.tr: I sent the money to Dad.

blocks.tip: “For you”: {{alang kanimo}}, or in everyday speech {{para nimo}}. Both are fine: {{Para nimo ni!}} “This is for you!”

mistakes.why: “To” a person is {{kang}}; {{si}} is for the focus.
After “to”, “me” is {{kanako}}.

lines.why: A place: {{sa}}. ({{kang}} is for people's names.)

options: Ihatag kang Lito. Para niya kana.

lessons.title: Say what you need and have to do
lessons.summary: Say “I need help”, “I have to go home” and “You don't have to pay.”
lessons.topic: {{kinahanglan}} + {{og}} (a thing), + a {{mo-}} verb, + an {{-on}} verb for a particular thing; {{dili kinahanglan}}

goal.t: Kinahanglan na ko mouli kay ulahi na.
goal.tr: I have to go home now because it's late.

dialog.tr: Joy, I have to go home now.
It's still early! Why?

dialog.t: Kinahanglan ko mobangon og sayo ugma. Naa koy trabaho.
dialog.tr: I have to get up early tomorrow. I have work.
I'll take you. I have a car.

dialog.t: Dili na kinahanglan, salamat. Mosakay lang ko og taxi.
dialog.tr: No need, thanks. I'll just take a taxi.

blocks.p: {{kinahanglan}} is “need”, “have to” or “must”. It works like {{gusto}}: with {{og}} and a thing, it's needing something ({{Kinahanglan ko og tabang.}} “I need help.”); with a {{mo-}} verb, it's having to do something ({{Kinahanglan ko mouli.}} “I have to go home.”).
**Don't have to.** {{dili}} in front, with the short word after it: {{Dili ka kinahanglan mobayad.}} “You don't have to pay.” And {{Dili na kinahanglan.}} on its own is “No need.”

**A particular thing.** When what you need is particular, point at it with {{ang}}, and the person comes from the {{nako}} set, as in a {{gi-}} sentence: {{Kinahanglan nako ang imong tabang.}} “I need your help.” If a verb follows, it takes its -on form from lesson 23: {{Kinahanglan nimong imnon ang tambal.}} “You need to take the medicine.”

ex.tr: I have to go home now.
You need to take the medicine.

blocks.tip: Softer than {{kinahanglan}}: {{angay}} “should” ({{Angay ka mopahulay.}}) and, from Spanish, {{dapat}} “should, ought to” ({{Dapat mopahulay ka.}}).

mistakes.why: The thing you need takes {{og}}.
After {{kinahanglan}}, as after {{gusto}}: {{mo-}}.
“Don't have to” is {{dili}}; {{wala}} is for what didn't happen.

practice.tr: I have to go home now.

practice.q: You're leaving a party. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: You're going home already? It's still early!

options: Oo, kinahanglan ko mobangon og sayo.
Oo, kinahanglan ko mibangon og sayo.

practice.q: Which one means “I need to rest”?

Your turn: say two things you have to do this week, and one you don't have to do.

answers.tr: I have to work on Saturday. I have to buy food. I don't have to get up early on Sunday.

answers.t: Kinahanglan ko motawag sa akong mama. Kinahanglan nakong limpyohan ang akong kwarto.
answers.tr: I have to call my mom. I have to clean my room.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Talk about food, places and hobbies you like and don't like.
lessons.topic: {{ganahan}} with the topic words ({{ganahan ko}}, {{ganahan siya}}) vs {{gusto}} with {{nako}}, {{niya}}; {{sa}} (what you like), {{og}} (an offer); {{pag-}}

goal.t: Ganahan kaayo ko sa lechon, pero dili ko ganahan sa durian.
goal.tr: I really like lechon, but I don't like durian.

dialog.tr: Do you like the food here?

dialog.t: Oo! Ganahan kaayo ko sa lechon ug sa puso.
dialog.tr: Yes! I really like lechon and puso.
And balut?
Oh, I don't like that!
Do you like swimming?

dialog.t: Ganahan kaayo ko molangoy, labi na sa Moalboal.
dialog.tr: I love swimming, especially at Moalboal.

blocks.p: {{ganahan}} is “like”. It's a describing word, so it takes the **topic words**: {{ganahan ko}}, {{ganahan ka}}, {{ganahan siya}}. That's different from {{gusto}}, which takes the {{nako}} set ({{gusto niya}}). Both are common, and both can mean “like” or “want”.

**What you like** takes {{sa}}: {{Ganahan ko sa lechon.}} “I like lechon.” With a pronoun, the short {{nimo}}, {{niya}} after {{ganahan ko}}: {{Ganahan ko nimo.}} “I like you.” With {{og}}, it's more like an offer of some: {{Ganahan ka og kape?}} “Would you like some coffee?”

**Liking to do something**: {{ganahan}} + a {{mo-}} verb ({{Ganahan ko molangoy.}} “I like to swim.”), or + {{sa}} + {{pag-}} ({{Ganahan ko sa paglangoy.}} “I like swimming.”). You met {{pag-}} in {{Unsaon pag-adto…?}}: it turns a verb into an “-ing” word.

ex.t: Ganahan ko sa prutas, labi na sa mangga.

blocks.tip: {{Dili ko ganahan ana.}} “I don't like that.” is polite enough; to turn down food gently, {{Busog pa ko, salamat.}} “I'm still full, thanks.” works even better.

lessons.title: Say what you can do and ask permission
lessons.summary: Say “I can speak a little Bisaya”, “I can't come”, “Do you know how to swim?” and “Can I sit here?”
lessons.topic: {{maka-}} “can, be able to”; {{kabalo}} “know how”; {{pwede}} and {{mahimo}} “may”; {{Wala ko kabalo.}}

goal.t: Makasulti ko og gamay nga Bisaya.
goal.tr: I can speak a little Bisaya.

dialog.tr: Do you speak Bisaya, Sir?

dialog.t: Gamay ra. Makasabot ko, pero lisud pa mosulti.
dialog.tr: Just a little. I can understand, but speaking is still hard.

Thanks! Can I taste this?

blocks.p: **Can, be able to: {{maka-}}.** Put {{maka-}} on the root: {{makasulti}} “can speak”, {{makaadto}} “can go”, {{makasabot}} “can understand”. {{Makaadto ka ugma?}} “Can you come tomorrow?” — {{Dili ko makaadto.}} “I can't come.” (Its “done” partner, {{naka-}}, comes in lesson 34.)

**Know how: {{kabalo}}.** For a skill you've learned, use {{kabalo}} + a {{mo-}} verb: {{Kabalo ka molangoy?}} “Do you know how to swim?” With languages there's a shortcut, {{mag-}} + the language's name: {{Kabalo ka mag-Bisaya?}} “Do you speak Bisaya?” And {{Wala ko kabalo.}} (with {{wala}}) is the everyday “I don't know.”

**May I? {{pwede}}** (or the more careful {{mahimo}}), + a {{mo-}} verb: {{Pwede ko molingkod dinhi?}} “Can I sit here?” {{Mahimo ba kong mangutana?}} “May I ask a question?” Answers: {{Pwede.}} / {{Sige.}} “Sure.” or {{Dili pwede.}} “You can't.”

lessons.title: Make plans with someone
lessons.summary: Invite a friend, agree on where and when: “Let's meet tomorrow at Ayala, at five.”
lessons.topic: {{kita}}/{{ta}} (with you) vs {{kami}}/{{mi}} (without you); {{mag-}}, the “not yet” of {{nag-}}, for doing things together

goal.t: Magkita ta ugma sa Ayala, alas singko.
goal.tr: Let's meet tomorrow at Ayala, at five.

dialog.tr: Lisa, are you free tomorrow?
Yes! What's the plan?
Shall we see a movie? There's a new one.
Sure! Where shall we meet?

dialog.t: Magkita ta sa Ayala, alas singko.
dialog.tr: Let's meet at Ayala, at five.
Is Joy coming?

dialog.t: Dili, moadto sila sa Bohol. Kita ra duha.
dialog.tr: No, they're going to Bohol. Just the two of us.

blocks.p: **Two “we”s, in real life.** Making plans with someone, it's always {{kita}} / {{ta}}, because they're included: {{Adto ta!}}, {{Magkita ta.}} Telling someone about you and other people, it's {{kami}} / {{mi}}: {{Moadto mi sa Bohol.}} “We're going to Bohol” (not you). Choosing wrong sounds like an invitation, or like leaving someone out!

**{{mag-}}: the “not yet” of {{nag-}}.** Just as {{mi-}} has {{mo-}}, {{nag-}} has {{mag-}}: {{Nagluto ko.}} “I cooked, I'm cooking.” → {{Magluto ko.}} “I'll cook.” {{mag-}} is also the usual form for doing something **together**: {{Magkita ta.}} “Let's meet (see each other).” {{Magdula ta.}} “Let's play.” {{Mag-istorya ta.}} “Let's talk.”
**{{mag-}} + a noun** means doing that activity: {{magsine}} “go to the movies” ({{sine}} is a movie), {{mag-Bisaya}} “speak Bisaya”. Very handy: {{Magsine ta?}} “Shall we go to the movies?”

ex.t: Moadto mi sa Bohol sa Sabado.
ex.tr: We're going to Bohol on Saturday.

blocks.tip: A plan with a question mark is a gentle suggestion: {{Magsine ta?}} {{Mokaon ta sa gawas?}} “Shall we eat out?” Answer {{Sige!}} “Okay!” or {{Dili ko makaadto, sorry.}}

mistakes.why: Inviting a friend includes them: {{ta}}. {{Adto mi}} would mean “We’re off” without them.
Tomorrow is not yet: {{mag-}}. {{nag-}} is done or going on.

lessons.title: Run errands and do chores
lessons.summary: Talk about shopping, laundry, dishes and meals: “I'm going shopping, then I'll do the laundry.”
lessons.topic: {{mang-}} (not yet) and {{nang-}} (done) for everyday activities: {{mamalit}}, {{manglaba}}, {{mangaon}}, {{mangutana}}; how {{mang-}} melts into the root

goal.t: Mamalit ko sa merkado, dayon manglaba ko.
goal.tr: I'm going shopping at the market, then I'll do the laundry.

dialog.tr: Ben, what are you doing today?

dialog.t: Mamalit ko sa merkado. Unsay akong paliton?
dialog.tr: I'm going shopping at the market. What should I buy?

dialog.t: Isda ug utanon. Ug manglaba pa ta unya.
dialog.tr: Fish and vegetables. And we still have to do the laundry later.

dialog.t: Sige. Human ana, mangaon ta sa gawas?
dialog.tr: Okay. After that, shall we eat out?

dialog.t: Sige, pero ikaw ang manghugas og plato!
dialog.tr: Okay, but you're washing the dishes!

blocks.p: **{{mang-}}** is a prefix for many everyday activities, especially ones done on several things or as a regular job: {{mamalit}} “go shopping” (buy things), {{manglaba}} “do the laundry”, {{manghugas}} “do the dishes”, {{mangaon}} “eat, have a meal”. Like {{mo-}} and {{mi-}}, it has a pair: {{mang-}} for not yet, {{nang-}} for done.

**{{mang-}} melts into the root.** Its last sound changes to fit the first sound of the root, which disappears: p and b become **m** ({{palit}} → {{mamalit}}), k becomes **ng** ({{kaon}} → {{mangaon}}), t and s become **n** ({{tan-aw}} → {{manan-aw}} “watch a show”). Before a vowel, h or l, it just adds on: {{manglaba}}, {{manghugas}}.

**Meals and asking** use it too: {{mamahaw}} “have breakfast”, {{maniudto}} “have lunch”, {{manihapon}} “have supper”, and from the Basics course {{mangutana}} “ask” and {{mangayo}} “ask for”. {{Mangaon na ta!}} “Let's eat!” is what you'll hear at every Bisaya table.

ex.tr: I'm going shopping at the market.
I'll do the laundry this Saturday.

ex.note: {{mo}} here is short for {{kamo}}, you all

lessons.title: Sound natural with little words
lessons.summary: Add the little words that give Bisaya its feeling: really, too, still, oh!, you know, of course.
lessons.topic: {{na}}, {{pa}}, {{lang}}, {{ra}}, {{gyud}}, {{sad}}, {{man}}, {{diay}}, {{baya}}, {{lagi}}, {{kaha}}

goal.t: Lami man diay ni!
goal.tr: Oh, this is actually tasty!

dialog.tr: Try this, Ben. Balut.
Oh, no thanks. I'm scared.
Just try it! Just a little.
…Hey, this is actually tasty!
Told you! One more?
Okay, one more!

blocks.p: Bisaya is full of small words that don't change the facts but change the **feeling**: surprise, insistence, softness, “me too”. You already know some. They gather right after the first word, with the short pronouns, so they're easy to drop in.

table: {{Kaon na!}} Eat now! {{Dili na.}} Not anymore.
{{Sayo pa.}} It's still early. {{Usa pa.}} One more.
{{Tubig lang.}} Just water. {{Duol ra.}} It's just near.
{{Asa man ka?}} So where are you? {{Maayo man.}} I'm fine.
{{Asa kaha siya?}} I wonder where she is.

blocks.p: **Two or three together** are normal: {{Lami man diay ni!}} “Oh, this is actually tasty!” {{Asa na man ka?}} “So where are you now?” Copy the orders you hear; the short pronouns {{ko}}, {{ka}}, {{ta}} usually come early in the group, and {{siya}}, {{sila}} later.

blocks.tip: {{sad}} is the Cebu word for “also, too” in conversation; you'll also hear {{pud}}, and see {{usab}} in writing. {{Mao ba?}} “Really?” and {{Mao diay?}} “Oh, really?” keep any conversation going.

mistakes.why: Nothing comes before it, so use the full {{ako}}: a short word can't start.
“Still” is {{pa}}; {{Sayo na}} would be “It's early now”.

lessons.title: Tell what happened, step by step
lessons.summary: Tell a friend about your trip in order: first, then, when we arrived, finally.
lessons.topic: {{mi-}}, {{nag-}}, {{gi-}} and {{nang-}} together in a story; {{una}}, {{dayon}}, {{unya}}, {{human ana}}, {{sa katapusan}}; {{pag-}} + root “when”

goal.t: Una, miadto mi sa baybayon. Dayon, naglangoy mi.
goal.tr: First, we went to the beach. Then we swam.

dialog.t: Kumusta ang inyong biyahe sa Bohol?
dialog.tr: How was your trip to Bohol?

dialog.t: Nindot kaayo! Una, misakay mi og barko alas sais sa buntag.
dialog.tr: Really nice! First, we took the boat at six in the morning.
And then?

dialog.t: Pag-abot namo, nag-abang mi og motor ug miadto sa Chocolate Hills.
dialog.tr: When we arrived, we rented a motorbike and went to the Chocolate Hills.
Did you see the tarsier?

dialog.t: Oo! Gamay kaayo! Unya, naniudto mi sa suba sa Loboc.
dialog.tr: Yes! So small! Then we had lunch on the river at Loboc.

dialog.t: Sa katapusan, mibalik mi sa Cebu alas otso sa gabii. Kapoy, pero lingaw!
dialog.tr: Finally, we came back to Cebu at eight at night. Tiring, but fun!

blocks.p: A story uses every “done” form you know, each for its own job: {{mi-}} for the events ({{misakay mi}} “we took the boat”), {{nag-}} for things that went on for a while ({{naglangoy mi}} “we swam, we were swimming”), {{gi-}} for particular things ({{gikaon namo ang sugba}} “we ate the grilled fish”), and {{nang-}} for errands and meals ({{naniudto mi}} “we had lunch”).
**Linking words** put the steps in order:

**When it happened: {{pag-}}.** {{pag-}} + a root + the person from the {{nako}} set means “when … (did it)”: {{Pag-abot namo…}} “When we arrived…”, {{Pag-uli nako…}} “When I got home…”. Word for word it's “at our arriving”, which is why the person is {{namo}}, {{nako}}.
**Said once is enough.** With {{ug}} “and”, the second verb can drop the person: {{Nag-abang mi og motor ug miadto sa Chocolate Hills.}} “We rented a motorbike and went to the Chocolate Hills.”

ex.tr: Then I took a shower and had breakfast.

ex.t: Pag-abot nako sa opisina, nagsugod na ang miting.
ex.tr: When I got to the office, the meeting had already started.

ex.t: Human ana, gitawagan nako si Mama.
Sa katapusan, natulog ko alas onse.
ex.tr: Finally, I went to bed at eleven.

blocks.tip: {{Kumusta ang…?}} “How was the…?” opens any story: {{Kumusta ang imong weekend?}} {{Kumusta ang biyahe?}}

lessons.title: Say what happened to you
lessons.summary: Say “I lost my phone!”, “It fell”, “It broke down”, and what you saw or heard.
lessons.topic: {{na-}} for what happens by accident or by itself ({{nawala}}, {{nahulog}}, {{naguba}}); {{ma-}} for what could happen; {{nakita}}, {{nadungog}}, {{nalimtan}}

goal.t: Nawala akong selpon!
goal.tr: I lost my phone!

dialog.tr: Oh no! My phone's gone!
What happened?

dialog.t: Ambot! Naa ra sa akong bag ganiha. Basin nahulog sa jeep.
dialog.tr: I don't know! It was in my bag earlier. Maybe it fell out in the jeepney.
Let's call it… Do you hear it?

dialog.t: Oo, nadungog nako! Naa ra diay sa akong bulsa!
dialog.tr: Yes, I hear it! It's in my pocket after all!
Oh, thank God!

blocks.p: **{{na-}}: it just happened.** For things that happen **by accident, or by themselves**, with nobody meaning to, Bisaya uses {{na-}}: {{nawala}} “got lost”, {{nahulog}} “fell”, {{naguba}} “broke down”, {{nabuak}} “smashed”, {{nabasa}} “got wet”. No doer is needed: {{Nahulog ang baso.}} “The glass fell.”

English says “I lost my phone”, as if you did it. Bisaya says what happened to the phone: {{Nawala akong selpon.}} “My phone got lost.” For something that **could** happen or is about to, use {{ma-}}: {{Mahulog na!}} “It's going to fall!”

**Seeing and hearing** happen to you too, so they use {{na-}}, with the person who sees or hears from the {{nako}} set, like a {{gi-}} verb: {{Nakita nako si Ben.}} “I saw Ben.” {{Nadungog nimo?}} “Did you hear (it)?” And forgetting: {{Nalimtan nako!}} “I forgot!”

ex.t: Nahulog sa yuta ang akong selpon.
ex.tr: My phone fell on the ground.
I got wet in the rain.

ex.t: Nakita ba nimo ang akong yawe?

blocks.tip: {{Hala!}} is the Bisaya “Oh no!” for small disasters; {{Salamat sa Dios!}} “Thank God!” when things turn out fine.

Seeing happens to you: {{na-}}, with the seer from the {{nako}} set.

lessons.title: Say what you've done, and what you never have
lessons.summary: Ask “Have you ever been to Bohol?”, answer “Once!” or “Not yet”.
lessons.topic: {{naka-}} (+ {{na}}) for experiences: {{Nakaadto ka na…?}}; {{wala pa}} + {{ka-}}; {{kausa}}, {{kaduha}}

goal.t: Nakaadto ka na sa Bohol? — Wala pa ko kaadto.
goal.tr: Have you ever been to Bohol? — I haven't been yet.

dialog.t: Emma, nakaadto ka na sa Bohol?
dialog.tr: Emma, have you ever been to Bohol?

dialog.t: Oo, nakaadto na ko didto kausa. Nindot kaayo!
dialog.tr: Yes, I've been there once. Really beautiful!
Have you ever eaten balut?

dialog.t: Wala pa! Ug dili gyud ko mokaon!
dialog.tr: Not yet! And I'm definitely not going to!
Have you ridden a habal-habal (motorbike taxi)?
Yes, twice now. Terrifying!

blocks.p: **{{naka-}}** is the done partner of {{maka-}} “can” (lesson 28): you **managed** to do it, or you've done it at some point. With {{na}}, it asks and tells about experiences: {{Nakaadto ka na sa Bohol?}} “Have you (ever) been to Bohol?” {{Nakaadto na ko.}} “I've been.” English needs “have been, have eaten”; Bisaya needs {{naka-}} and {{na}}.

**Not yet, never.** {{wala pa}} + {{ka-}} + the root: after {{wala}}, {{naka-}} shrinks to {{ka-}}: {{Wala pa ko kaadto.}} “I haven't been yet.” Add {{gyud}} for “never”: {{Wala pa gyud ko kaadto.}} “I've never been.”
**How many times**: {{kausa}} once, {{kaduha}} twice, {{katulo}} three times; {{pila ka beses?}} how many times?; {{daghan na ka beses}} many times.

**Managed to, could.** Without {{na}}, {{naka-}} and {{wala … ka-}} are about one occasion: {{Nakatulog ka?}} “Did you get some sleep?” {{Wala ko kaadto tungod sa ulan.}} “I couldn't go because of the rain.”

ex.t: Nakaadto na ko sa Manila, pero wala pa ko kaadto sa Davao.
ex.tr: I've been to Manila, but I haven't been to Davao yet.

ex.t: Kausa ra ko nakasakay og eroplano.
ex.tr: I've only been on a plane once.

ex.t: Wala ko kaadto tungod sa ulan.
ex.tr: I couldn't go because of the rain.

blocks.tip: In fast speech you may hear {{Wala pa ko nakaadto}}, keeping the whole {{naka-}}. People understand it; {{Wala pa ko kaadto}} is the standard.

mistakes.tr: Have you ever been to Bohol?
mistakes.why: To ask “Have you ever been…?”, use {{naka-}}. {{Miadto ka na sa Bohol?}} asks whether they’ve already left for Bohol.
After {{wala}}, {{naka-}} shrinks to {{ka-}}.

lessons.title: Say when, and for how long
lessons.summary: Say how long you've been somewhere, since when, and when something happened or will happen.
lessons.topic: Number + {{ka}} + time + {{na}} “for … now”; {{sukad}} “since”; {{dugay}}; {{kanus-a}}; {{… ang milabay}} “ago”; {{kaniadto}}

goal.t: Tulo ka tuig na ko dinhi sa Cebu.
goal.tr: I've been here in Cebu for three years.

dialog.tr: When did you come to Cebu?

dialog.t: Tulo ka tuig na ang milabay. Tulo ka tuig na ko dinhi.
dialog.tr: Three years ago. I've been here three years.

dialog.t: Dugay na diay! Asa ka nagpuyo kaniadto?
dialog.tr: That's a long time! Where did you live before?

dialog.t: Sa Chicago. Napulo ka tuig ko didto.
dialog.tr: In Chicago. I was there for ten years.
When are you going home to America?
I don't know! Maybe never!

blocks.p: **For how long, up to now.** A number + {{ka}} + the time + **{{na}}**: {{Tulo ka tuig na ko dinhi.}} “I've been here three years.” The little {{na}} makes it “up to now”; English needs “have been”. Without {{na}}, the time is over: {{Napulo ka tuig ko didto.}} “I was there for ten years.”

**Since: {{sukad}}.** {{sukad sa 2020}} “since 2020”, {{sukad pa sa bata ko}} “since I was a child”. **Long**: {{Dugay na.}} “It's been a long time.” {{Dugay ka na dinhi?}} “Have you been here long?” {{Dili pa dugay.}} “Not long.”

**When.** {{kanus-a}} with {{mi-}} for the past ({{Kanus-a ka miabot?}}) or {{mo-}} for the future ({{Kanus-a ka mobalik?}}). “Ago” is {{ang milabay}} after the time: {{duha ka adlaw ang milabay}} “two days ago”. And {{kaniadto}} is “before, in the old days”: {{Nagpuyo ko sa Davao kaniadto.}} “I used to live in Davao.”

{{sulod sa duha ka adlaw}} in two days
