lessons.title: Say how you feel (at the doctor's)
lessons.summary: Say you're hungry, tired or sick, what hurts, and how you feel: happy, sad, angry, missing someone.
lessons.topic: Body states with {{gi-}} ({{gigutom}}, {{gikapoy}}, {{gihilantan}}); feelings with {{na-}} ({{nalipay}}, {{nasuko}}); {{sakit}} + a body part

goal.t: Gihilantan ko, ug sakit akong ulo.
goal.tr: I have a fever, and my head hurts.

dialog.tr: Good morning. How are you feeling?

dialog.t: Gihilantan ko sukad gahapon, Doc. Ug sakit kaayo akong ulo.
dialog.tr: I've had a fever since yesterday, Doc. And my head really hurts.
Do you have a cough?

dialog.t: Gamay ra. Pero gikapoy kaayo ko.
dialog.tr: Just a little. But I'm really tired.

dialog.t: Trangkaso lang ni. Imna kini nga tambal tulo ka beses sa usa ka adlaw, ug pahulay.
dialog.tr: It's just the flu. Take this medicine three times a day, and rest.
Thank you, Doc.

blocks.p: **The body: {{gi-}}.** States of the body take {{gi-}} and work like describing words: first, then the person. {{Gigutom ko.}} “I'm hungry.” {{Gikapoy siya.}} “She's tired.” {{Gihilantan ang bata.}} “The child has a fever.”

**Feelings: {{na-}}.** Emotions take {{na-}}, the “it happened to me” prefix of lesson 33: {{Nalipay ko.}} “I'm glad.” {{Nasubo siya.}} “She's sad.” {{Nasuko si Mama.}} “Mom is angry.” {{Nahadlok ko.}} “I'm scared.” And missing someone is {{gimingaw}}: {{Gimingaw ko nimo.}} “I miss you.”

**Pain: {{sakit}}** + the body part: {{Sakit akong ulo.}} “My head hurts.” {{Sakit akong tiyan.}} “My stomach hurts.” {{Unsay sakit?}} “What hurts?” Body words: {{ulo}} head, {{tiyan}} stomach, {{likod}} back, {{tutunlan}} throat, {{tiil}} foot, {{kamot}} hand.

ex.tr: I'm thirsty. Is there any water?

blocks.tip: {{Unsay imong gibati?}} is “How do you feel?”, word for word “What do you feel?”. To a friend, simply {{Okay ra ka?}} “Are you okay?”

mistakes.why: {{gutom}} is the noun “hunger”; “hungry” is {{gigutom}}.
The describing word first, as always.

practice.tr: I'm thirsty. Is there any water?

options: Sakit akong tutunlan, ug giubo ko.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.summary: Say what's bigger, cheaper or nicer, what's the best, and “How beautiful!”
lessons.topic: {{mas}} … {{kaysa}} “more … than”; {{pinaka-}} “the most”; {{parehas}} “the same”; {{ka-}} + describing word “How …!”

goal.t: Mas init sa Cebu kaysa sa Baguio.
goal.tr: It's hotter in Cebu than in Baguio.

dialog.t: Asa man ang mas nindot, Bohol o Siargao?
dialog.tr: Which is nicer, Bohol or Siargao?

dialog.t: Para nako, mas nindot ang Siargao. Pero mas duol ang Bohol.
dialog.tr: For me, Siargao is nicer. But Bohol is closer.
And the food?
Both just as delicious!

dialog.t: Asa ang pinakanindot nga baybayon sa Cebu?
dialog.tr: Which is the most beautiful beach in Cebu?

dialog.t: Para nako, ang Malapascua. Kanindot didto!
dialog.tr: For me, Malapascua. It's so beautiful there!

blocks.p: **More: {{mas}}.** Put {{mas}} before the describing word: {{mas dako}} “bigger”, {{mas nindot}} “nicer”, {{mas mahal}} “more expensive”. Bisaya never changes the word itself, so there's nothing like “-er” or “better” to learn.

**Than: {{kaysa}}**, with {{sa}} before a noun or place ({{kaysa sa Baguio}}) and the “to” words before a pronoun ({{kaysa kanako}} “than me”). In everyday talk the {{kaysa}} part is often dropped: {{Mas taas siya kanako.}} “She's taller than me.”

**The most: {{pinaka-}}**, joined to the word: {{pinakadako}} “the biggest”, {{pinakanindot}} “the most beautiful”. Before a noun it links with {{nga}}: {{ang pinakanindot nga baybayon}} “the most beautiful beach”. ({{labing}} means the same: {{labing nindot}}.)

**The same: {{parehas}}.** {{Parehas ra.}} “It's the same.” {{Parehas mi og edad.}} “We're the same age.” {{Parehas ra kalami.}} “Just as delicious.” And {{ka-}} + a describing word is an exclamation: {{Kanindot!}} “How beautiful!”, {{Kainit!}} “It's so hot!”, {{Kamahal!}} “So expensive!”

ex.tr: This one is bigger than that one.

ex.t: Mas barato dinhi kaysa sa mall.
ex.tr: It's cheaper here than at the mall.
This is the most beautiful beach.

blocks.tip: {{Asa ang mas…?}} “Which is more…?” uses {{asa}}, “where”, for “which of two”: {{Asa ang mas barato?}} “Which one is cheaper?”

mistakes.tr: This one is bigger than that one.
mistakes.why: Comparing needs {{mas}} before the describing word.

mistakes.tr: This is the most beautiful beach.
mistakes.why: {{pinaka-}} joins the word, and {{nga}} links it to the noun.

lessons.title: Give reasons
lessons.summary: Explain why: “I didn't go because it was raining”, “That's why…”, “so that…”.
lessons.topic: {{kay}} and {{tungod kay}} “because”; {{tungod sa}} “because of”; {{mao nga}}, {{busa}} “so, that's why”; {{aron}} “so that”

goal.t: Wala ko moadto kay nag-ulan.
goal.tr: I didn't go because it was raining.

dialog.t: Nganong wala ka moadto sa party gahapon?
dialog.tr: Why didn't you come to the party yesterday?

dialog.t: Kay gihilantan ko. Mao nga natulog ko og sayo.
dialog.tr: Because I had a fever. That's why I went to bed early.

dialog.t: Ay, sorry! Okay na ka karon?
dialog.tr: Oh, sorry! Are you okay now?

dialog.t: Oo, mas maayo na. Miinom ko og tambal aron mamaayo dayon.
dialog.tr: Yes, better now. I took some medicine so I'd get well fast.

dialog.t: Maayo kay naa pay laing party sa Sabado!
dialog.tr: Good, because there's another party on Saturday!

dialog.t: Tungod niana, kinahanglan gyud ko mamaayo!
dialog.tr: Because of that, I really have to get better!

blocks.p: **Because: {{kay}}**, before a whole sentence: {{Wala ko moadto kay nag-ulan.}} It also starts the answer to {{Ngano?}}: {{Kay gikapoy ko.}} “Because I'm tired.” {{tungod kay}} means the same, a little more carefully. Before a **noun**, “because of” is {{tungod sa}}: {{tungod sa ulan}} “because of the rain”.
**So, that's why: {{mao nga}}** (or {{busa}}, more formal), before the result: {{Gikapoy ko, mao nga mouli na ko.}} “I'm tired, so I'm going home.”

**So that: {{aron}}**, for the purpose, usually with a {{maka-}} or {{ma-}} verb: {{Nagtuon ko aron makapasar.}} “I studied so that I'd pass.” {{Mobangon ko og sayo aron dili ko maulahi.}} “I'll get up early so I won't be late.”

ex.t: Wala ko kaadto tungod sa ulan.
ex.tr: I couldn't go because of the rain.

ex.t: Gikapoy ko, mao nga mouli na ko.
ex.tr: I'm tired, so I'm going home.

ex.t: Nagtuon ko og maayo aron makapasar.
ex.tr: I studied hard so that I'd pass.
It rained, so we didn't go out.

ex.t: Mobangon ko og sayo aron dili ko maulahi.
ex.tr: I'll get up early so I won't be late.

blocks.tip: In casual Cebu talk you'll also hear {{kay}} used almost like “is”: {{Ang Cebu kay nindot.}} “Cebu, it's beautiful.” That's a different {{kay}}; you only need to recognize it.

mistakes.wrong: Wala ko moadto tungod sa nag-ulan.
mistakes.right: Wala ko moadto tungod kay nag-ulan.
mistakes.tr: I didn't go because it was raining.
mistakes.why: Before a whole sentence: {{kay}} or {{tungod kay}}. {{tungod sa}} goes before a noun ({{tungod sa ulan}}).

mistakes.wrong: Mao nga gikapoy ko, natulog ko.
mistakes.right: Gikapoy ko, mao nga natulog ko.
mistakes.tr: I was tired, so I went to sleep.
mistakes.why: {{mao nga}} goes before the result, not the reason.

I couldn't go because of the rain.

lessons.title: Say which one you mean
lessons.summary: Point out people and things by what they do: “the woman who's singing”, “the bus that goes to Lahug”, “the one cooking”.
lessons.topic: {{nga}} + a doer verb: {{ang babaye nga nagkanta}}; {{ang nagluto}} “the one who cooked”; {{hain}} “which one”

goal.t: Kinsa ang babaye nga nagkanta? — Akong igsoon.
goal.tr: Who's the woman who's singing? — My sister.

dialog.t: Kinsa kadtong lalaki nga nagsul-ob og pula?
dialog.tr: Who's that guy wearing red?
That's Lito, my neighbor.
And the woman who's singing?

dialog.t: Iyang asawa. Ug ang mga bata nga nagdula sa gawas, ilang mga anak.
dialog.tr: His wife. And the kids playing outside are their children.
So which one is your husband?
The one grilling the fish!

blocks.p: To say **which** person or thing you mean, put {{nga}} and a verb after the noun: {{ang babaye nga nagkanta}} “the woman who's singing”, {{ang bus nga moadto sa Lahug}} “the bus that goes to Lahug”. One word, {{nga}}, does the work of English “who”, “which” and “that”: it's the same linker that joined describing words in lesson 11.

blocks.means: a part of a sentence with its own verb, like “who's singing” in “the woman who's singing”.

blocks.p: **The verb keeps its form**: {{nag-}} for what's going on ({{nga nagkanta}} “who's singing”), {{mi-}} for what happened ({{nga miabot gahapon}} “who arrived yesterday”), {{mo-}} for what will happen or happens regularly ({{nga moadto sa Lahug}} “that goes to Lahug”). In this lesson the person or thing **does** the action; lesson 42 adds “the book that I read”.
**“The one who…”**: leave out the noun. {{ang nagluto}} “the one who cooked”, {{kadtong nagluto}} “that one who's cooking” ({{kadto}} + -ng), {{ang mga miadto}} “the ones who went”.
**Which one? {{hain}}.** {{Hain man ang imong bana?}} “Which one is your husband?” {{Hain ang imoha?}} “Which one is yours?” ({{imoha}} is “yours”, {{akoa}} is “mine”.)

ex.t: Kinsa ang lalaki nga nagsul-ob og pula?
Asa ang bus nga moadto sa Lahug?
ex.tr: Where's the bus that goes to Lahug?

ex.t: Siya ang tawo nga nagtabang nako.
ex.tr: He's the person who helped me.
The one who's cooking is my husband.

ex.t: Ang mga bata nga nagdula sa gawas, akong mga apo.
ex.tr: The kids playing outside are my grandchildren.

blocks.tip: A sentence can start with the long description, pause, then say what it is: {{Ang babaye nga nagkanta, akong igsoon.}} “The woman who's singing, that's my sister.” Very natural in speech.

mistakes.why: Link the noun and its verb with {{nga}}.

mistakes.wrong: Asa ang bus nga miadto sa Lahug?
mistakes.right: Asa ang bus nga moadto sa Lahug?
mistakes.tr: Where's the bus that goes to Lahug?
mistakes.why: A bus that goes there (regularly, or next): {{mo-}}. {{miadto}} would be “that went”.

lessons.title: Say what will happen if…
lessons.summary: Make plans that depend on something: “If it rains tomorrow, we won't go”, “When you arrive, call me.”
lessons.topic: {{kung}} + {{mo-}} “if”; {{inig}} + root “when (it happens)”; {{pag-}} “when (it happened)”; {{kung}} for habits

goal.t: Kung moulan ugma, dili ta moadto sa baybayon.
goal.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go to the beach.

dialog.tr: Are we still on for tomorrow?
Yes, if it doesn't rain.
And if it rains?

dialog.t: Kung moulan, manan-aw na lang ta og sine.
dialog.tr: If it rains, we'll just watch a movie.

dialog.t: Sige. Inig abot nako sa imong balay, tawagan tika.
dialog.tr: Okay. When I get to your house, I'll call you.

dialog.t: Sige! Kung gigutom ka, naa koy luto.
dialog.tr: Okay! If you're hungry, I've cooked something.

blocks.p: **If: {{kung}}.** For something that may or may not happen, {{kung}} + a {{mo-}} verb (it hasn't happened): {{Kung moulan ugma…}} “If it rains tomorrow…”. The other half is a plan ({{dili ta moadto}}) or a command ({{tawagi ko}}). {{kung}} works with every kind of sentence you know: {{Kung naa kay oras…}} “If you have time…”, {{Kung gigutom ka…}} “If you're hungry…”, {{Kung gusto nimo…}} “If you want…”.

**When, in the future: {{inig}}** + the root + the person from the {{nako}} set: {{Inig abot nimo, tawagi ko.}} “When you arrive, call me.” It's the future twin of the {{pag-}} you used in stories: {{Pag-abot nimo…}} “When you arrived…”. (In everyday speech {{pag-}} is often used for the future too; {{inig}} is the careful way.)
**Whenever.** For habits, {{kung}} means “when, whenever”: {{Kung Domingo, mosimba mi.}} “On Sundays, we go to mass.” {{Kung init, molangoy ko.}} “When it's hot, I go swimming.”

ex.t: Kung moulan ugma, dili ta moadto.
ex.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.

ex.t: Kung naa kay pangutana, tawagi ko.
ex.tr: If you have a question, call me.
When I get home, I'll cook.
On Sundays, we go to mass.

blocks.tip: {{Kung dili ko masayop…}} “If I'm not mistaken…” is a polite way to correct someone or to share something you're not sure of.

mistakes.right: Kung moulan ugma, dili ta moadto.
mistakes.tr: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
mistakes.why: It hasn't happened: {{mo-}}.
After {{inig}}, just the root, then the person.

lessons.title: Put events in order: before, after, while
lessons.summary: Say what happens before, after, while and until: “Before you go out, close the windows.”
lessons.topic: {{human sa}} “after”; {{sa dili pa}} / {{sa wala pa}} “before”; {{samtang}} “while”; {{hangtod}} “until”

goal.t: Sa dili pa ka mogawas, sirad-i ang mga bintana.
goal.tr: Before you go out, close the windows.

dialog.t: Ben, mobiya na ko. Sa dili pa ka mogawas, sirad-i ang mga bintana.
dialog.tr: Ben, I'm leaving now. Before you go out, close the windows.
Okay, Mom. When are you coming back?

dialog.t: Human sa akong miting, mga alas singko.
dialog.tr: After my meeting, around five.

dialog.t: Samtang wala ka, magluto ko sa panihapon.
dialog.tr: While you're out, I'll cook supper.

dialog.t: Salamat! Pero ayaw sa kaon hangtod moabot ko.
dialog.tr: Thanks! But don't eat until I get back.
Okay, but don't take too long, Mom!

blocks.p: **After: {{human sa}}** + a noun ({{human sa klase}} “after class”, {{human sa akong miting}} “after my meeting”) or a {{pag-}} word ({{human sa pagkaon}} “after eating”). You know {{human ana}} “after that” from stories.

**Before.** For what hasn't happened yet, {{sa dili pa}} + the person + a {{mo-}} verb: {{Sa dili pa ka mogawas…}} “Before you go out…”. For the past, {{sa wala pa}}, still with {{mo-}}, just as {{wala}} always takes it: {{Sa wala pa ko moadto sa Cebu, nagpuyo ko sa Manila.}} “Before I came to Cebu, I lived in Manila.” The little {{pa}} is “yet”: word for word “while not yet going out”.

**While: {{samtang}}.** {{Nagkanta siya samtang nagluto.}} “She sang while she cooked.” {{samtang wala ka}} “while you're away”. **Until: {{hangtod}}**, before a time or a verb: {{hangtod alas siyete}} “until seven”, {{hangtod moabot ko}} “until I arrive”.

ex.t: Human sa pagkaon, nanghugas siya og plato.
ex.tr: After eating, she did the dishes.

ex.t: Sa dili pa ka mobiya, tawagi ko.
Sa wala pa ko moadto sa Cebu, nagpuyo ko sa Manila.
ex.tr: Before I came to Cebu, I lived in Manila.

blocks.tip: {{Ayaw sa!}} “Not yet! Wait!” uses the {{sa}} “first, for now” of lesson 19: {{Ayaw sa kaon.}} “Don't eat yet.”

mistakes.wrong: Sa dili pa ko miadto sa Cebu, nagpuyo ko sa Manila.
mistakes.right: Sa wala pa ko moadto sa Cebu, nagpuyo ko sa Manila.
mistakes.tr: Before I came to Cebu, I lived in Manila.
mistakes.why: Before something in the past: {{sa wala pa}}, and after {{wala}} the verb is {{mo-}}.
{{human}} + {{sa}} + the noun.

lessons.title: Point out who did it
lessons.summary: Say “It was Dad who cooked”, “I'll pay”, and “the cake my grandma made”.
lessons.topic: Putting the person first: {{Si Papa ang nagluto.}}; {{nga}} with a {{gi-}} verb: {{ang libro nga akong gibasa}}

goal.t: Kinsa ang nagluto niini? — Si Mama ang nagluto.
goal.tr: Who cooked this? — Mom did.

dialog.t: Lami kaayo ang adobo! Kinsa ang nagluto?
dialog.tr: The adobo is so good! Who cooked it?

dialog.t: Si Papa ang nagluto. Ako ang namalit sa merkado.
dialog.tr: Dad cooked it. I did the shopping at the market.

blocks.p: **The spotlight.** To say **who** did something, put the person first and {{ang}} before a doer verb: {{Si Papa ang nagluto.}} “It was Dad who cooked, Dad cooked it.” {{Ako ang mobayad.}} “I'll pay (it's me who'll pay).” It answers {{Kinsa ang…?}} “Who…?” in the same shape.

**The thing done to.** In lesson 39, {{nga}} pointed at the doer: {{ang babaye nga nagluto}} “the woman who cooked”. To point at the **thing** instead (“the cake my grandma made”, “the book I read”), the verb after {{nga}} must point at it too: a {{gi-}} verb. {{ang cake nga gihimo sa akong lola}}, {{ang libro nga akong gibasa}}.

This is a real Bisaya rule: {{nga}} can only point at the verb's focus. So **the verb's prefix decides** what the description is about. And the doer of the {{gi-}} verb often comes **before** it, as {{akong}}, {{imong}}, {{iyang}}: {{ang libro nga akong gibasa}} = {{ang libro nga gibasa nako}}.

table: {{ang babaye nga nagluto sa adobo}} the woman who cooked the adobo
{{ang adobo nga giluto sa babaye}} the adobo the woman cooked

{{ang awto nga iyang gipalit}} the car he bought
{{Si Papa ang nagluto.}} Dad cooked it.
{{Adobo ang giluto ni Papa.}} It was adobo that Dad cooked.

lessons.title: Pass on what someone said
lessons.summary: Tell people what someone said or asked: “Ben said he'd be late. He says he's arriving at seven.”
lessons.topic: {{miingon}} … {{nga}}; {{daw}} / {{kuno}} “they say, apparently”; {{matud pa ni}} “according to”; {{nangutana kung}} “asked if”

goal.t: Miingon si Ben nga ulahi siya. Moabot daw siya alas siyete.
goal.tr: Ben said he'd be late. He says he'll arrive at seven.

dialog.tr: So where's Ben?

dialog.t: Nitawag siya ganiha. Miingon siya nga ulahi siya kay grabe ang trapiko.
dialog.tr: He called earlier. He said he'd be late because the traffic is terrible.
So when does he say he'll get here?

dialog.t: Alas siyete daw. Ug nangutana siya kung naa pa tay lechon.
dialog.tr: Seven, he says. And he asked whether we still have lechon.

dialog.t: Ingna siya nga naa pa, pero dali lang!
dialog.tr: Tell him there is, but to hurry!

blocks.p: **Said that: {{miingon}} … {{nga}}.** Put what was said after {{nga}}: {{Miingon siya nga ulahi siya.}} “He said he'd be late.” Bisaya keeps the words the way the speaker said them: no “would”, no change of tense, because the verbs never showed time anyway. In speech you'll also hear just {{Ingon siya…}}.
**Telling someone**: {{Ingna siya nga…}} “Tell him that…” ({{ingna}} is the command of {{ingon}}), {{Gisultihan ko niya nga…}} “She told me that…” (the {{-an}} verb of lesson 24).

**{{daw}} (or {{kuno}}): they say, apparently.** Bisaya marks news that came from someone else with one little word after the first word: {{Moabot daw siya alas siyete.}} “He says he'll arrive at seven.” {{Nindot daw ang sine.}} “They say the movie's good.” It's everywhere in conversation. Who said it: {{matud pa ni Mama}} “according to Mom”, {{matud pa niya}} “according to him”.

**Asked if, asked where.** {{nangutana}} “asked” + {{kung}} “whether, if” for a yes-or-no question ({{Nangutana siya kung naa ka.}} “She asked if you were there.”), or + the question word ({{Nangutana siya kung asa ka.}} “She asked where you were.”).

ex.t: Matud pa ni Mama, mouli ta og sayo.
ex.tr: According to Mom, we're going home early.

ex.t: Gisultihan ko niya nga ganahan siya nimo!
ex.tr: She told me she likes you!

blocks.tip: {{daw}} is also how gossip travels: {{Minyo na daw siya!}} “Apparently she's married now!” Add {{kuno}} when you doubt it a little.

mistakes.why: Join what was said with {{nga}}.

mistakes.tr: She asked if you were there.
mistakes.why: A passed-on yes-or-no question takes {{kung}} “whether, if”.

lessons.title: Give your opinion
lessons.summary: Say what you think, agree and disagree politely, and say how sure you are.

goal.t: Para nako, mas lami ang lechon sa Cebu kaysa sa Manila.
goal.tr: For me, Cebu lechon is tastier than Manila's.

dialog.t: Unsa imong hunahuna, asa ang mas lami nga lechon, Cebu o Manila?
dialog.tr: What do you think, where's the tastier lechon, Cebu or Manila?

dialog.t: Para nako, mas lami ang sa Cebu. Dili na kinahanglan og sarsa!
dialog.tr: For me, Cebu's is tastier. It doesn't even need sauce!

dialog.tr: I agree with you! And mangoes?

dialog.tr: Maybe you're right. Let's taste both!

blocks.p: **What you think.** Start with {{Sa akong hunahuna,…}} “I think, in my opinion” (word for word “in my thinking”), {{Para nako,…}} “For me…”, or {{Sa akong tan-aw,…}} “The way I see it…”. To ask: {{Unsa imong hunahuna?}} “What do you think?”
**Agree, disagree.** {{Uyon ko.}} “I agree.” {{Uyon ko nimo.}} “I agree with you.” {{Dili ko uyon.}} “I don't agree.” {{Tama ka.}} “You're right.” {{Sakto!}} “Exactly!”

**How sure you are.** {{murag}} “it seems, it looks like”: {{Murag moulan.}} “It looks like rain.” {{Murag lami.}} “It looks tasty.” Maybe: {{tingali}}, {{siguro}} (from Spanish) and {{basin}} “might”: {{Basin ulahi siya.}} “He might be late.” And {{Dili ko sigurado.}} “I'm not sure.”

ex.t: Sa akong hunahuna, maayo kana nga plano.
ex.tr: I think that's a good plan.

ex.t: Para nako, mas nindot ang Moalboal.

ex.tr: It looks like it'll rain this afternoon.

blocks.tip: Disagreeing gently is the Cebu way: {{Tingali tama ka, pero…}} “Maybe you're right, but…” works much better than a flat {{Sayop ka.}} “You're wrong.”

lessons.title: Ask for favors and get things done
lessons.summary: Say “Let me see”, “Could I borrow your charger?”, “Excuse me, let me through”, and “I'll have my phone fixed.”
lessons.topic: {{pa-}} “let, have someone do”: {{Patan-awa ko.}}, {{Pahulama ko…}}; {{ipa-}} and {{magpa-}} for getting something done

goal.t: Pahulama ko sa imong charger, palihug.
goal.tr: Could I borrow your charger, please?

dialog.t: Joy, pahulama ko sa imong charger, palihug. Patay na akong selpon.
dialog.tr: Joy, could I borrow your charger, please? My phone is dead.

dialog.t: Sige, ania. Ug patan-awa ko sa imong mga litrato sa Bohol!
dialog.tr: Sure, here. And let me see your Bohol photos!

dialog.t: Unya na lang. Guba sad ang akong screen; ipaayo nako ugma.
dialog.tr: Later. My screen is broken too; I'm having it fixed tomorrow.
Where are you having it fixed?

dialog.t: Sa mall. Ug magpaputol ko og buhok didto.
dialog.tr: At the mall. And I'll get a haircut there too.
Let me come with you! I'll do some shopping there.

blocks.p: **{{pa-}}: let, have.** The prefix {{pa-}} means letting or having someone do something. Its handiest use is the polite **“let me…”**: {{pa-}} + root + {{-a}} + {{ko}}. {{Patan-awa ko.}} “Let me see.” {{Patilawa ko.}} “Let me taste.” {{Pahulama ko sa imong ballpen.}} “Let me borrow your pen.” {{Paagia ko.}} “Let me through.” Even {{palihug}} “please” is built this way.
**Borrow and lend** are one word in Bisaya, {{hulam}}: {{Pahulama ko og kwarta.}} “Lend me some money.” (word for word “let me borrow money”).

**Getting something done** by someone else: {{ipa-}} points at the thing ({{Ipaayo nako ang akong selpon.}} “I'll have my phone fixed.” {{Gipaayo nako.}} “I had it fixed.”), and {{magpa-}} / {{nagpa-}} points at you ({{Nagpaputol ko og buhok.}} “I got a haircut”, word for word “I had hair cut”).

ex.t: Asa ka nagpatahi sa imong sinina?
ex.tr: Where did you have your dress made?

blocks.tip: In a crowded jeepney or market, a quiet {{Paagi, palihug}} or {{Paagia ko}} gets you through politely.

mistakes.why: Asking to borrow: “let me borrow”, {{pa-}} + root + {{-a}} + {{ko}}.
The shop fixed it for you: {{pa-}}. {{Giayo nako}} means you fixed it yourself.

lessons.title: Wish and hope
lessons.summary: Say “I hope it doesn't rain”, “I hope you're well”, and “someday, God willing”.
lessons.topic: {{unta}} “I hope, hopefully”; {{hinaut nga}}; {{puhon}} “God willing”; {{unta}} to soften a request

goal.t: Unta dili moulan ugma!
goal.tr: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow!

dialog.t: Ugma na ang atong biyahe sa Camiguin!
dialog.tr: Our trip to Camiguin is tomorrow!

dialog.t: Unta dili moulan. Murag naay bagyo.
dialog.tr: I hope it doesn't rain. It looks like there's a typhoon.

dialog.tr: Hopefully not! I hope we get to see dolphins.

dialog.tr: God willing. And I hope there aren't too many people at the beach.

dialog.tr: As long as I'm with you, it'll be fun!

blocks.p: **{{unta}}: I hope, hopefully.** Put it at the start of the sentence, which keeps its usual verb ({{mo-}} for what's still to come): {{Unta dili moulan.}} “I hope it doesn't rain.” {{Unta makapasar ko.}} “I hope I pass.” Like the other little words, it can also sit after the first word: {{Moabot unta siya.}} “I hope he comes.”

**{{hinaut nga}}** means the same, a little more heartfelt, and joins with {{nga}}: {{Hinaut nga maayo ka.}} “I hope you're well.” **{{puhon}}** is “God willing, someday”, said about any plan or dream: {{Mobalik ko, puhon.}} “I'll come back, God willing.” You'll hear it every day in Cebu.
**Softening a request.** {{unta}} also makes a request gentler, like English “perhaps” or “could I possibly”: {{Pwede unta ko mangayo og tabang?}} “Could I perhaps ask for some help?”

ex.tr: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.
I'll come back to Cebu someday, God willing.

ex.t: Pwede unta ko mangayo og tabang?
ex.tr: Could I perhaps ask for some help?

blocks.tip: With a done verb, {{unta}} turns into “should have, would have”: {{Mitawag unta ka!}} “You should have called!” That's the next lesson.

{{hinaut}} joins the rest with {{nga}}.

lessons.title: Imagine what would happen
lessons.summary: Imagine and regret: “If I had lots of money, I'd buy a house”, “If I were you…”, “If only I'd known!”
lessons.topic: {{kung}} … {{pa}}, then {{mo-}} + {{unta}} “would”; {{kung ako pa nimo}} “if I were you”; done verb + {{unta}} “would have, should have”

goal.t: Kung naa pa koy daghang kwarta, mopalit unta ko og balay duol sa dagat.
goal.tr: If I had lots of money, I'd buy a house by the sea.

dialog.t: Kung daghan ka og kwarta, unsa imong buhaton?

blocks.p: **Imagining.** For something that isn't true now, start with {{kung}} (often with {{pa}}), and put {{unta}} in the result with a {{mo-}} verb: {{Kung naa pa koy daghang kwarta, mopalit unta ko og balay.}} “If I had lots of money, I'd buy a house.” {{mo-}} + {{unta}} is English “would”.
**If I were you**: {{Kung ako pa nimo,…}}, word for word “if I were still you”: {{Kung ako pa nimo, mopahulay ko.}} “If I were you, I'd rest.”

**The past that didn't happen.** Use a done verb in both halves: {{kung}} + a done form + {{pa (lang)}}, then {{mi-}} + {{unta}} for “would have”: {{Kung nahibal-an pa lang nako, miadto unta ko.}} “If only I'd known, I would have gone.” On its own, a done verb + {{unta}} is a regret or a reproach: {{Mitawag unta ka!}} “You should have called!”

table: {{Kung naa pa koy oras, mouban unta ko.}}
If I had time, I'd come along.

{{Kung nahibal-an pa lang nako, miadto unta ko.}}
If I'd known, I would have gone.

blocks.tip: {{Sayang!}} “What a waste, what a shame!” is the word for missed chances, and you'll hear it after every “if only”.

blocks.p: This last lesson puts the whole course to work. Telling your own story is something Cebuanos will ask for again and again ({{Unsay imong istorya?}}), and it uses nearly everything you've learned. Each part has its lesson, if you want to look back:

table: {{Mibalik ko kay nalipay kaayo ko dinhi.}}

blocks.p: **Keep the verbs straight**: {{mi-}} and {{nag-}} for what happened, {{nag-}} for your life now, {{mo-}} and {{mag-}} for plans, {{naka-}} for experiences, {{gi-}} when a particular thing is in focus. And the little words ({{na}}, {{pa}}, {{gyud}}, {{sad}}) make it sound like you.

ex.t: Taga-Canada ko, pero nagpuyo na ko sa Cebu.
ex.tr: I'm from Canada, but I live in Cebu now.

ex.t: Niadtong 2022, miadto ko dinhi sa unang higayon.
ex.tr: In 2022, I came here for the first time.

ex.t: Nalipay kaayo ko sa mga tawo, mao nga mibalik ko.
ex.tr: I loved the people, so I came back.

ex.t: Karon, nagtrabaho ko sa usa ka eskwelahan sa Mandaue.
ex.tr: Now I work at a school in Mandaue.

ex.t: Nakaadto na ko sa daghang isla, pero ang Bohol gihapon ang akong paborito.
ex.tr: I've been to lots of islands, but Bohol is still my favorite.

ex.t: Unta makasulti ko og Bisaya sama sa usa ka lumad.
ex.tr: I hope I can speak Bisaya like a native.

blocks.tip: Practice your story out loud until it comes out without stopping. Then tell it to someone in Cebu: it's the best way to start a long conversation, and people will love that you tried.

mistakes.wrong: Tulo ka tuig ko dinhi na.
mistakes.right: Tulo ka tuig na ko dinhi.
mistakes.why: {{na}} and {{ko}} gather right after the first phrase ({{tulo ka tuig}}).

mistakes.wrong: Kung madawat ang akong aplikasyon, nagsugod ko sa sunod tuig.
mistakes.right: Kung madawat ang akong aplikasyon, magsugod ko sa sunod tuig.
mistakes.tr: If my application is accepted, I'll start next year.
mistakes.why: Next year is not yet: {{mag-}}.

practice.t: Upat ka tuig ___ ang milabay, mibakasyon ko dinhi.
practice.tr: Four years ago, I came here on vacation.
practice.why: {{X ka tuig na ang milabay}}: X years ago.

practice.t: Nalipay kaayo ko, ___ nga mibalik ko.
practice.tr: I loved it, so I came back.

practice.q: A new friend asks about your life. Choose your replies.

lines.t: Kanus-a ka nagsugod og tuon og Bisaya?
lines.tr: When did you start studying Bisaya?

options: Usa ka tuig na ang milabay.
Usa ka tuig pa ang milabay.
Kay gusto ko makaistorya sa akong mga silingan.
Aron gusto ko makaistorya sa akong mga silingan.
Salamat! Unta mas maayo pa sa sunod tuig.
Salamat! Kung mas maayo pa sa sunod tuig.

practice.q: Say “I've been studying Bisaya for a year.”
practice.answer: Usa ka tuig na ko nagtuon og Bisaya.

practice.q: Say “If I have time, I'll come back next year.”
practice.answer: Kung naa koy oras, mobalik ko sa sunod tuig.

practice.q: Your turn: tell your own story: where you're from, what brought you to Bisaya, what you do now, and one hope.

answers.t: Taga-Amerika ko. Duha ka tuig na ang milabay, nakaila ko og usa ka Cebuana, ug karon akong asawa na siya. Nagtrabaho ko sa usa ka opisina, ug nagtuon ko og Bisaya matag adlaw. Unta makaistorya ko sa iyang pamilya sa Pasko, puhon!
answers.tr: I'm from America. Two years ago, I met a woman from Cebu, and now she's my wife. I work in an office, and I study Bisaya every day. I hope I can talk with her family at Christmas, God willing!

answers.t: Taga-England ko, pero nagpuyo ko sa Cebu sukad pa sa 2023. Miabot ko kay ganahan ko sa dagat. Karon nagtudlo ko og diving sa Moalboal. Gusto ko magpabilin dinhi hangtod sa akong pagkatigulang!
answers.tr: I'm from England, but I've lived in Cebu since 2023. I came because I love the sea. Now I teach diving in Moalboal. I want to stay here until I'm old!
